spans.text: Developing people     /     ARTICLE 27
Help a team think strategically

A program team sees more calls asking for the status of service inquiries and proposes assigning another employee to answer the phone. Before anyone moves staff, ask the group to work through the decision together. Strategic thinking involves observing what is happening, analyzing the choices, drawing and testing inferences, hearing other people’s reasoning and solving the problem that the evidence supports. Each of those skills can be practiced in an ordinary team meeting.
Work through a decision with evidence in view

Begin with an observation the team could verify. How many people called, over what period, and about which stage of the process? Count repeat contacts separately from distinct inquiries if the available records permit it. An increase in calls could reflect a longer wait, an unexpected notice or a contact number that now sends more people to this team. Ask someone to identify which of these explanations the existing information can distinguish.

Next, look at how the facts constrain a choice. A staff transfer might shorten time on hold but lengthen the queue that prompted the calls. A clearer update might help someone who is waiting for a routine response but do little for someone with an urgent need. Invite the staff handling the inquiries and those receiving the transfers to explain what each option would change during a typical shift. Ask about an earlier attempt and which conditions have changed since then.
Make the reasoning available to the next team

Choose a small action that can teach the group something. The team could try a clearer status message for one category of inquiries and compare the pattern of follow-up contacts over a defined period. Agree in advance on who can authorize the change, what would justify expanding it and what would prompt the team to stop. A promising result may still depend on time of year or on who received the new message.

Keep the decision, assumptions, observations and follow-up date together in the appropriate work records. Follow the agency’s guidance for retaining records and handling personal information. When another unit sees a similar pattern, it can examine the reasoning, identify what transfers to its situation and avoid repeating a choice whose conditions no longer hold.
Shared or distributed leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
27    Help a team think strategically
Make two explanations compete for the same evidence

For the team facing an increase in status calls, consider two plausible explanations. Under the first, requests are moving through the program more slowly. Under the second, requests move at the usual pace, but people have stopped receiving an acknowledgment with a reliable estimate of the next contact. Both explanations fit a full phone queue. They would lead the team to spend scarce staffing time differently. Name one observation you would expect under each. Then look for the information that would help the team distinguish the two.

Use Equity dashboards: from display to decisions to practice reading what a measure includes. A count of completed calls tells you about callers who got through. It cannot tell you how many people tried repeatedly and abandoned the call, or who used a trusted partner instead. A high completion rate in a small category can be especially hard to interpret. Before comparing groups, establish the time period, the denominator and how much information is missing. Work through the authorized data channels and give the decision maker only the detail the decision calls for.
Decide what to do while several explanations remain plausible

A manager could assign another worker to phones for a short period to protect access while a second team examines acknowledgments. Give the arrangement an explicit review date and a question worth answering. Did repeat status calls drop after people began receiving clearer information? Did adding phone capacity shorten waits but move a backlog to another part of the process? Identify whose experience can illuminate each measure. A partner organization may hear from people who never reach the team; a front-line worker can show what a person sees when their request enters the system.

Strategic perspective develops when a leader can explain both an immediate action and how it affects other parts of the organization. Participative leadership brings in knowledge that a central dashboard cannot provide. Procedural discipline keeps the group’s record of its decision usable after a staff change. Save the reasons for the choice, including the evidence that would lead the team to reverse or modify it, in an appropriate shared location. A colleague taking over the pilot should be able to see why another explanation was set aside.

Try applying the same sequence to a favorable result. If requests are completed faster, examine whether people understand the outcome and can reach someone about a mistake. A decision can improve speed while creating new work elsewhere. Leaders who go looking for that possibility are teaching colleagues a method they can use again.
Development capability. Examine assumptions and use evidence.

pages.title: Use participation where people can shape a decision

spans.text: Developing people     /     ARTICLE 28
Use participation where people can shape a decision

A manager wants to improve how community partners reach a program team. They can invite feedback on the current contact route, ask partners to help design alternatives or ask them to choose among options. These invitations give people different degrees of influence. Explain which one you are making before anyone spends an evening preparing comments. People can contribute to a decision they disagree with when they understand the question, their role and how the final choice was made.
Decide whose experience the team needs

Start with the actual choice and the limits around it. For example, the program may have to use existing staffing but may be able to change when callbacks are offered. Identify who will gain or lose access under different schedules. Include people who handle the calls, partners who make referrals and people who try to use the route without a partner. Ask how they would like to take part. One advisory member cannot describe every user’s experience.

Design participation around the question. A small workshop can compare alternatives and expose tradeoffs. Individual interviews may reveal problems someone would hesitate to raise in front of a supervisor. A short written response can give people time to check an idea with others. Arrange accessible formats and communication supports, and allow time for replies. An experienced facilitator can help when authority, competing interests or a difficult history make a group discussion hard to run fairly.
Show what happened to the contributions

Suppose people on a fixed work schedule say that a broadly worded promise of a daytime callback makes it hard to answer. Ask what a more usable arrangement would require. Test any proposed time window with the staff who must cover it and the people who would receive the call. Give both groups a chance to identify a difficulty the other may not have seen.

When the manager makes the decision, report which suggestions changed it, which could not be adopted and why. Name a point when people can report how the new arrangement works in practice. A person who helped design it should be able to recognize where their experience entered the decision and who owns the next adjustment.
Democratic or participative leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
28    Use participation where people can shape a decision
Choose a way of working that fits the public decision

A short survey, a discussion with a facilitator and a joint design session invite very different contributions. If the team needs to know which of three existing contact routes partners can actually use, a short comparison followed by interviews may be sufficient. If none of the three routes works for many people, a vote among them locks the group into an inadequate choice. Invite people to describe a recent attempt and show where it broke down. That evidence can help the team develop another option before asking anyone to choose.

Meaningful community engagement for leaders includes practice in identifying who is absent and in hearing disagreement without losing its meaning. Apply it before invitations go out. Write a paragraph explaining which parts of a service decision can still change and who will make the choice. Read it as a person who has missed three callbacks, a family member supporting someone who prefers to speak for themselves, and a program worker who will maintain the new arrangement. Which of those people would recognize a reason to take part? Which might need a different time, format or contact route? Confirm these needs with participants.
Give a facilitator a question with an honest answer

Human-centered design can help a group examine the steps a person takes and try an alternative. Appreciative inquiry can surface a practice that already succeeds under difficult conditions. A consensus workshop can help participants organize possibilities and discover common ground. Choose the method based on the decision, the people affected and the authority they have been given. If the sponsor will make the final choice, explain the grounds on which they will weigh competing needs. A capable facilitator can prevent one voice from dominating a meeting. They cannot give a group decision authority that the sponsor has withheld.

Consider a partner who objects to the proposed callback arrangement because it would exclude people who cannot take private calls during a shift. A participant may disagree and value a predictable appointment. Preserve the reason for both positions in the record. “Participants preferred appointments” would omit evidence needed to consider a fallback contact method. Bring the record back in a form participants can correct, and give the person who decides time to respond before launch.

When a decision is unpopular, a supervisor can exercise participative leadership by explaining whose evidence changed the design and which constraint prevailed. Acknowledge the concern that remains unresolved and who can revisit it. Treat the quality of influence as an outcome. People should be able to recognize their contribution in the reasoning even when their preferred option was set aside.
Development capability. Connect equity with workforce decisions.

pages.title: Use authority in service of others

spans.text: Developing people     /     ARTICLE 29
Use authority in service of others

A leadership title changes what you can authorize, whose call is returned and which concerns reach a director. Servant leadership asks how you use that access on behalf of the people doing and receiving the work. Minnesota’s 2019 creation of the One Minnesota Council on Inclusion and Equity gave public expression to a commitment to inclusion. A supervisor can give that commitment practical meaning in a specific decision and accept responsibility for the result.
Let the people who experience a barrier help define it

Imagine a notice has gone out announcing community listening sessions, and an interested resident asks how to participate from home. The department already has a busy calendar of in-person sessions. Before calling the request a scheduling problem, ask the resident what participation would require and whether they would like to hear about alternatives. Ask the staff organizing the sessions which constraints they can address and which require a manager’s decision.

A supervisor can use their position to secure staff time, raise an access need with the event owner or ask for a revised plan. Let the colleagues who understand the logistics shape the options and let the resident decide whether an option is useful to them. If a change will take time, identify who can answer questions in the meantime. Taking over every conversation can leave everyone dependent on the supervisor the next time a barrier appears.
Account publicly for the decisions within your control

If you approved the original schedule, acknowledge that decision and the participation it made difficult. Explain what you changed, who will follow up and how people will hear whether the arrangement worked. An apology carries weight when the person can see the repair. Protect a resident’s privacy when describing a lesson to colleagues. A team can learn from the gap without identifying the person who first pointed it out.

Carry what you learned into the next planning discussion. Ask staff whose experience they still need and whether their usual method of seeking input can reach those people. Keep learning about the communities affected by the team’s work and invite correction when your understanding is incomplete. The responsibility to act on what you learn belongs to you as well as to the people who were willing to teach you.
Servant leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
29    Use authority in service of others
Serve a person who disagrees with the offer of help

Imagine a planning session where a staff member and a relative do most of the speaking while the person seeking services uses a communication device. A well-intentioned leader may wish to shorten the meeting by completing their sentences or asking the relative to choose among the options. Start by asking the person how they want to communicate, who they want involved and what would make the discussion workable. Make time for their answer. A person’s decision to involve someone they trust can be an exercise of their authority. A professional decision to substitute someone else’s judgment changes who is directing the conversation.

The application course Centering people with disabilities in decision-making takes the learner through participation arrangements, preparation and support, as well as how to keep someone’s priorities visible when other people assist. Use it to prepare an alternative to a hurried planning session. Offer the questions in advance and arrange a way for the person to contribute privately, with support or over more than one contact when feasible. Confirm with them which words they want recorded and where the team will carry their input. Explain any formal decision or eligibility question that remains with an authorized person.
Spend authority on the obstacle the person cannot remove

A supervisor might be able to change the meeting schedule, arrange an accessible document or reserve staff time to follow up. The resident cannot fix those agency arrangements by being more assertive. Use your authority to remove a specific obstacle and be clear about the part you cannot approve. If a different office controls the resource, find the responsible contact, obtain permission before sharing personal details where needed and take responsibility for returning with an answer. A promise to advocate carries little value if the person is sent from one contact to the next to find out whether it happened.

Servant leadership and supported decision-making raise an important tension. An energetic leader can make things happen quickly and still crowd out the person whose life the decision concerns. Inclusive leadership helps the group hear what has been overlooked. Ethical leadership helps the supervisor own unintended harm and explain the remedy. Ask a colleague to observe whether staff interrupt, whom they address when the person uses support and whose words appear in the final account. Discuss the observations without making assumptions about anyone’s identity or capacity.

If the person later says the account missed what mattered, reopen the part the team can change and identify the proper route for the rest. A revised record and a real change in how the next conversation proceeds are concrete evidence that the organization received the correction.
Development capability. Build inclusion and accessibility into work.

spans.text: Developing people     /     ARTICLE 30
Influence through example and opportunity

A supervisor asks staff to use plain language when writing to the public, then circulates a memo full of unexplained abbreviations. The team receives two lessons. One is the instruction in the memo. The other is the language that appears to earn approval. Colleagues who lead work without a title face a similar choice every time they prepare an example, respond to a question or recommend someone for an assignment.
Make the practice visible enough to borrow

Choose a passage that often confuses a reader and show how you would revise it. For example, a sentence might tell people to contact an office about a change in circumstances. Work with the person who knows the procedure to specify which changes matter, who can help and what information someone should have ready. Ask a colleague unfamiliar with the process to describe the action the revised sentence calls for. Use their answer to improve the wording.

Share the two versions and explain the decisions behind them. Give credit to the subject expert and the reader who found the remaining ambiguity. A colleague in another unit can now borrow the method for a different notice. They can also see that accuracy still matters when making a sentence easier to read. This is how a small choice can influence work beyond the original team.
Notice who gets the next opportunity

A person who identified the difficulty may be ready to facilitate the next review. Ask about their interest and what support they want. Recommend them by naming the contribution you observed and the part of the assignment it prepares them to handle. Give them a chance to make decisions and to present the result in their own words. Doing so transfers both responsibility and recognition.

Watch for the habits your own influence may be spreading. If you regularly thank only the person who delivers the final presentation, colleagues may learn to overlook the people who made the work accurate. If you acknowledge a correction made by a newer colleague, other supervisors can see what happens when expertise is recognized across ranks. Invite someone who receives your messages to tell you which example they are actually following.
Charismatic leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
30    Influence through example and opportunity
Make the reasoning visible so a good practice can travel

A colleague who circulates an excellent plain-language memo has offered a useful example. Colleagues may copy the wording without understanding which features mattered. Make one editorial decision visible. Suppose the first draft said that inquiries would be “routed to the appropriate unit.” The revision says who receives the inquiry, how the person will hear back and what they can do if the expected contact does not occur. Explain how the change answers the reader’s next practical question. A worker can reuse that reasoning in a different program even when the route and the words must change.

In Mentoring and peer learning, the learner works on an example, hears another person’s reasoning and uses a question to make their own revision. Use that sequence with two colleagues. One brings a short public instruction stripped of personal information. The other reads it as a resident trying to act on it and explains where they stopped. The author chooses one revision and says what problem it addresses. A peer’s role is to help make the choice visible. Final approval for public instructions remains with the people who have it.
Notice which practices your influence is rewarding

The fastest response to a high-profile request may come from the person who routinely works late. If a supervisor repeatedly praises the speed of that response and gives the same person every subsequent assignment, the team may learn that availability outside normal hours is a condition of influence. Others cannot copy that practice on equal terms. Recognize the judgment that improved the response and arrange working time for others to practice it. Credit the colleague who identified a confusing passage, including when someone else presented the finished revision.

A charismatic leader can attract attention to a useful change. Influence is more likely to survive their absence if colleagues understand why the change helped and can make their own decisions. A distributed approach gives the next review to someone with knowledge of the audience and enough authority to carry out the task. Tell them what they may change, who can authorize publication and whom they can consult. If they recommend a different solution, judge it against the person’s ability to use the instruction.

After two teams have tried the method, ask each to bring one example of an improvement and one example where the model did not transfer cleanly. A phrase that works for a scheduled follow-up might confuse someone who has no appointment. Learning where a practice needs adaptation keeps good intentions from spreading a new set of mistakes across the organization.
Development capability. Communicate and facilitate across difference.
Direction and priorities     /     ARTICLE 31
Leading through an administrative transition

A new administration takes office on a particular day. The work of answering questions, paying vendors and keeping appointments carries on through it. For the staff member who knows which partner to call when a referral goes missing, the most valuable contribution to a transition may be making that knowledge available to someone else. For an incoming director, it may be finding out which quiet arrangements have kept a service working before deciding what to change.
What the outgoing team can leave behind

Choose one service that people depend on every week. Trace it from the first contact to the last commitment. Identify who can make a decision, who has promised what to whom, and where the next person can find the record. Write down pending choices with their deadlines and the consequences of delay. Ask a colleague unfamiliar with the service to use the handoff to answer a real work question. Their first unanswered question tells you what the packet still needs.

During a transition, people can be at different points in letting go of earlier work, finding their footing and committing to what comes next. William Bridges’s transition model gives managers language for those experiences. Set a time for regular updates, even when a decision is pending. A useful update might be, “The schedule for next week stands. The new assignment is awaiting a decision. On Thursday I’ll tell you whether we have one.” Staff can act on each part of that message.
What an incoming leader needs to learn

The STARS framework, as applied to government by Peter Daly and Michael Watkins, distinguishes starting a new operation, turning around a struggling one, realigning work with new conditions and sustaining a successful effort. A single division may have different assignments in different units. Ask each team what must endure, what has stopped working and what evidence supports that assessment. A call queue that looks slow may include time spent arranging the next contact so a caller can actually use it.

Set one three-month outcome and ask staff and partners how they would recognize progress. Give individual contributors a place to raise a continuity risk or correct an incomplete handoff. When the team tries a change, agree on what would justify keeping, adjusting or reversing it. That gives a new leader room to learn while people can still count on the service.

A new leader can use a Plan–Do–Study–Act cycle on a single handoff. Predict what the new contact arrangement will change, try it with one team, compare the result with the prediction and use what happened to choose the next adjustment. Name both the operational outcome and the experience staff and partners should have while reaching it.
Adaptive and situational leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
31    Leading through an administrative transition
What a supervisor can responsibly say on Monday

Suppose an email announces a review of outreach contracts. A worker tells a partner that next month’s session has been cancelled. Another worker assures a family that the session will happen as planned. Both heard the same news. One believed that moving early would protect people from disappointment. The other believed that a calm reassurance would keep a relationship intact. Neither had established what the review actually changed. A leader who simply tells the team to “be consistent” leaves them to choose between two equally unsupported answers.

In Leading with values when guidance shifts, work through the lesson on identifying the actual change. Write the sentence you can support from the communication, who issued it, and the part of the service it addresses. Next to it write the question the email leaves open. In the example, determine who can confirm whether the existing session is affected. Give a named worker the follow-up and agree when the partner needs a response. If several programs depend on the session, arrange one update that reaches them all. The continuity decision is now visible to the person who must make it.
Change your approach when the decision changes hands

Before the decision, a participative approach helps a new manager learn which arrangements people are relying on. A directive response has a different use when a mistaken cancellation is already circulating. The manager can direct staff to correct the inaccurate message, within their authority, while keeping open the question of what happens next month. Trying to reach team consensus about the status of the contract would give participants responsibility for a decision they cannot make.

An outgoing manager has another task. Ask the worker who knows the partner to lead the first update with a successor listening. At the next update reverse their roles. Notice whether the successor knows about the partner’s lead time, preferred contact route and fallback contact without prompting. That is evidence of knowledge transfer. The incoming director can then review a concise record of what staff have promised, what remains open and who owns the next decision. A resident should not have to rebuild the relationship for the agency every time leadership changes.
Development capability. Share knowledge and build future capability.

pages.title: Managing a public budget through the year

spans.text: Direction and priorities     /     ARTICLE 32
Managing a public budget through the year

A program manager opens the monthly report and sees spending below plan. Has the team saved money, or has an invoice simply not arrived? The answer matters if colleagues are already counting on those dollars for interpretation, staff training or contract work. A manager brings knowledge of what the team has promised. Fiscal colleagues bring knowledge of how commitments appear in the accounts and what the funding permits. A budget conversation needs both.
Read the difference between a plan and a payment

Ask the fiscal team to walk through the Manager’s Financial Report for your area. Managers with the appropriate access can use SWIFT to obtain it. Pick one line that differs materially from the forecast. Establish what period it covers, what has posted, what is committed and which costs are still expected. Ask about the program calendar. A quarter with little spending can be entirely predictable if a partner bills after a major deliverable.

Consider a unit that expected eight facilitated sessions by June. Six have taken place, the invoice covers four, and two sessions are still scheduled. Three different quantities matter here: sessions planned, sessions delivered and sessions paid for. Before treating the balance as available, reconcile all three with the contract lead. If demand changed, update the forecast and tell the people whose work depends on it.
Decide what the variance calls for

A vacant position may produce salary savings while colleagues carry extra work. A training balance may mean that nobody can leave the phones during business hours. Ask what the figures mean for staff and for service. The useful decision might be to arrange coverage so employees can attend training, revise an unrealistic estimate, or ask finance whether a one-time expenditure fits the funding terms. A favorable balance alone gives no one authority to commit funds to another purpose.

Choose a review rhythm that matches risk and activity. Record the amount in question, the explanation, the person who will confirm it and the next date to review it. Learn where the program sits in the agency and state budgets so you can explain a proposed expenditure in terms of the public purpose it serves.
Ethical leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
32    Managing a public budget through the year
Compare who can use the dollars

A manager has a small one-time balance and two credible proposals. One would cover additional daytime information sessions that an established contractor can start immediately. The other would pay for an evening pilot with interpretation and preparation time for a smaller partner. The first proposal predicts a lower cost per seat. The second may reach people who have been unable to attend. The manager should be able to describe the choice accurately even if the higher-volume option ultimately wins.

Use Equity in rate setting and budget decisions to practice reading a distribution alongside an average. For each proposal, distinguish seats available, people likely to attend, people reached for the first time and people who can use the information afterward. Mark estimates as estimates. The evening partner may know what attendance has looked like elsewhere, yet still need time to learn how this particular group would respond. Compare how each figure was obtained and which costs have been included. A budget that assumes a community organization will coordinate for free conceals a real cost by moving it off the agency’s ledger.
Give the recommendation a fair hearing

An ethical leader makes the reason for favoring an option available for challenge. A procedural approach establishes who verifies restrictions, approves spending and reviews a contract. A participative approach brings the affected people into the question of what a useful session would provide. Each addresses a different problem. A well-attended meeting cannot authorize spending, and fiscal approval gives little evidence about what a participant will experience.

Draft a recommendation in four sentences. State the public purpose, the two competing uses, the evidence supporting the preferred option, and the uncertainty the decision maker must accept. Include an estimate of staff time. If a supervisor chooses the evening pilot, someone needs to release a worker from another assignment to run it. Once the sessions take place, compare attendance and participant experience with the forecast. Ask who encountered a barrier and what the team can change next cycle. If the balance was spent on time but the intended residents remained unable to participate, the fiscal record can be correct while the service design still needs work.
Development capability. Connect equity with workforce decisions.

spans.text: Direction and priorities     /     ARTICLE 33
Leading change across an organization

Imagine that several units agree to accept referrals through one shared route. At the design meeting, the proposal looks simpler for everyone. At a local partner’s office, a worker is wondering who will answer when someone cannot use that route. At the receiving unit, staff are asking who will own an urgent referral when information is incomplete. Both questions belong in the design of the change. Finding them after launch leaves the people with the fewest choices to work around the problem.
Give the people doing the work decisions to make

Assemble a group that can follow a referral across the whole service. Include someone who sends it, someone who receives it and people who can describe the process of seeking help. Give members a clear charge. For example, leadership may have set the goal of one point of entry while leaving contact methods and handoff procedures open. Spell out which decisions the group owns, which it can recommend and who can resolve a conflict. Arrange ways for people to contribute around work schedules or outside a large meeting.

Ask each person to trace the same difficult case. Compare where responsibility changes hands. If a partner sees no way to confirm that a referral arrived, make that a design question. Explain why the change is being made, the next decision and the person who can answer operational questions. Publish the answer wherever staff will need it during a shift.
Watch what survives first contact with practice

Pilot the change on a scale where the team can notice and repair a failure. Check how many referrals reach a named worker and how often a person seeking help has to start again. Debrief with both units. If staff quietly return to a previous process, find out what it allowed them to accomplish. An informal phone call may have prevented someone from being stranded between offices. Retain that function in the new arrangement.

Thank the colleagues who made the earlier system work and the person who points out a defect in the new one. Show what the group changed in response. Staff learn whether leaders welcome difficult news by watching what happens to the first person who brings it.

An organization can invite criticism on a pilot and still discourage it in practice. Ask pilot staff who have seen a flaw to choose a workable way to raise it, give someone the authority to pause or adjust a failing step and explain afterward which observation led to a change. That sequence gives people evidence that leaders will protect room for learning during the rollout.
Shared or distributed leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
33    Leading change across an organization
Trace what a change asks each unit to give up

Return to the shared referral route. A program manager announces that every unit will use it beginning next month. A receiving supervisor says their team is ready because every worker has access to the system. A county partner says it cannot send urgent information through the new route. An intake worker adds that a telephone handoff has been the only reliable way to confirm that someone in crisis was connected. These are different accounts of readiness. Choosing the most senior person’s account could turn a project milestone into a service failure.

In Coordinating policy changes across units, follow the lesson on tracing a revision through connected work. Use one ordinary referral and one urgent referral as separate examples. Give each unit a chance to explain what it receives, what it can do with that input and how the next person knows it has accepted responsibility. Have the partner make the same journey from outside the agency. Give each unresolved handoff an owner with authority to settle it or a route to someone who can.
Give staff a way to change the rollout

Transformational leadership can keep people focused on the experience the new arrangement should deliver. Shared leadership puts parts of the design with people who have the needed knowledge. A sponsor might give the receiving unit responsibility for proposing an acknowledgment method and the partner group a real choice about how to receive it. The sponsor should say which common service expectations still apply and how two units can resolve competing requests. A committee with no decisions of its own offers little protection against a flawed design.

At the midpoint, ask what evidence would justify continuing, revising or briefly holding the rollout. For example, sample whether a sender can determine who has the referral without a second call. Check the urgent cases separately because a good overall rate can hide a serious problem in a small group. Give staff time and permission to surface failed transfers while there is still time to repair them. Report back to the pilot group with the change made in response, the decision maker and what happens to the old route. That closes an operational gap that enthusiasm at a launch meeting could never resolve.
Development capability. Build inclusion and accessibility into work.

pages.title: Turning a strategic priority into a plan

spans.text: Direction and priorities     /     ARTICLE 34
Turning a strategic priority into a plan

Suppose a division wants Minnesotans to get a useful answer the first time they ask for help. One leader proposes a new website. Another proposes adding people to the phones. Before committing to either, the team needs to know what a useful answer means to the people calling, who can change the experience, and which competing work it is prepared to defer. Strategic planning gives staff and partners a way to make those choices together.
Establish the purpose and examine the current experience

The sponsor can begin by naming the decision the plan will guide, the people who can commit resources and the constraints the group will face. Invite staff who receive questions and partners who hear what happens afterward. Ask each person to describe a recent contact that worked well and one that required a second attempt. Compare those accounts with available service data. A short call might mean the question was answered quickly. It might also mean the caller was referred elsewhere and still needs help.

Identify what you know well enough to act on, what remains uncertain and whose experience is missing. Give one person responsibility for filling a consequential evidence gap. Time spent gathering more information should reflect how much it could change the decision.
Choose a direction and give the first steps owners

Return to the program’s mission to check that the ambition fits its purpose. Picture the difference people could experience in three to five years. Choose a small number of strategies the team can pursue over the next year or two, then assign actions for the next three to six months. For example, if workers in two units give conflicting answers, reconcile those answers and test a common response before investing in a new contact channel.

Write the first assignment so the person taking it can tell when it is done. Name who can approve a corrected answer, when front-line staff will try it and how the team will learn whether it helped. At the next planning meeting, review what happened to the people seeking help. If the evidence changes the team’s view of the problem, make the adjustment visible to the people who helped set the direction.

Use appreciative inquiry when part of the service already works well. Invite a worker and a partner to reconstruct a successful contact and identify which conditions made it possible. Decide which of those conditions the strategy could reproduce elsewhere and what additional evidence would be needed before doing so.
Adaptive and situational leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
34    Turning a strategic priority into a plan
Negotiate what would count as improvement

In a planning session, three units endorse the goal of answering more questions on first contact. They mean different things. One counts a call routed to the right unit as answered. Another counts it only when a worker explains the next step. A resident who has received the same referral twice may judge success by whether the receiving office actually responds. A plan that leaves all three definitions in place could report improvement while staff and residents experience continuing difficulty.

Use Setting equity measures and targets to work through the lesson on the recorded event. Ask each unit to show which event its available information captures and what the record leaves unknown. Agree on a measure people can interpret today and a method for learning about the missing part. A short, optional follow-up with a small group of callers might reveal whether the answer was usable. A finding from that small group can inform a decision without supporting a claim about every caller. Identify who could be systematically missed, including people who never get through the queue.
Choose a first investment under constraint

The team has capacity for one pilot. Digital staff propose revised search terms to help residents find an answer on the website. Program staff propose a pilot that connects callers directly to a receiving unit. Use an adaptive leadership approach when the teams hold different beliefs about what successful access looks like. Give each a chance to show where its proposal would make the greatest difference and which residents would still encounter difficulty. Then have the named decision maker choose a pilot and state the reason. A choice to try one option now should leave the other team clear about what future evidence would reopen the decision.

Translate the pilot into a short agreement. Identify the service group, the baseline observation, the person responsible for implementation, the source of follow-up information and the date of the first adjustment. If the team can document faster routing but cannot yet establish whether residents received an answer, report both facts. Strategic leadership includes resisting pressure to declare success simply because the activities in the plan have been completed.
Development capability. Examine assumptions and use evidence.

pages.title: Setting a vision people can use

spans.text: Direction and priorities     /     ARTICLE 35
Setting a vision people can use

Two teams may agree on their purpose and still disagree about what to fund next. A mission explains why the work exists. A vision describes a future the organization hopes to bring about. Its value shows up when two worthwhile choices compete for the same time or money. Ask whether a colleague could use the proposed vision to choose between them and explain that choice to a person affected by it.
Start with a scene from the future

Invite colleagues and people with experience of the service to picture an ordinary day three to five years from now. What would someone trying to reach the right worker be able to do? What would a new employee see an experienced colleague doing differently? Collect individual answers before opening the discussion so the first person to speak has less influence over what others consider possible. Give people another way to contribute if they prefer to write or need more time.

Suppose one person imagines leaving a call knowing who owns the next step. Another pictures being able to communicate in the way that works for them. A third wants staff to see whether help actually arrived. List the specific changes embedded in those answers. A small drafting group can bring back language that captures the shared ambition. Let participants say what the draft gets right, what it drops and whether anyone would read it as a promise the organization cannot keep.
Try the words against a real choice

A candidate vision for this exercise might be, “People who contact us know who will follow up, when to expect an answer and how to reach us if the plan changes.” Give the group two proposals: redesign the home page or give receiving teams a reliable way to confirm a handoff. Ask which would move practice closer to the envisioned experience and what evidence would change their answer. Either could be right under different conditions.

Use the agreed wording when setting priorities and when explaining a decision to staff. Revisit it as community needs and program responsibilities change. If nobody can point to a decision it has influenced, bring a specific upcoming choice back to the group and see where the language needs work.
Transformational leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
35    Setting a vision people can use
Hear what people mean by the same promise

Suppose a division chooses “responsive service” as its ambition. To a phone worker that means answering quickly. To a disability advocate it means a caller can use the channel they choose. To a partner with a complex question it may mean one person remains responsible until a usable answer arrives. A leader can gather unanimous support for those two words and still have no agreement about what a Tuesday afternoon should look like. Ask people to supply the experience behind the word they support.

Team values that guide real decisions offers a way to examine competing meanings of a shared word. Apply it to a choice between a rapid callback promise and a longer appointment with a person who can resolve several questions. For each option, ask who gains time, who must do more work and which part of the agency promise the option keeps. Where a person needs an accessible way to participate, identify the responsible process and resources. A general vote about customer preferences would leave that particular obligation unresolved.
Give people a way to challenge the picture

A charismatic presentation may draw attention to a goal. The test comes after the presentation, when a supervisor must decide which kind of contact staff are rewarded for completing. If the supervisor recognizes only the shortest calls, workers learn a narrower meaning of responsiveness than the director described. Invite a staff member to show one instance where the performance measure and the vision point in different directions. The director should name who can change that measure and invite a practical alternative.

Transformational leadership can give people a shared sense of direction across units. A transformative or equity-centered approach adds a question about the rule itself. Who selected speed as the only visible sign of a good service, who has been carrying the cost, and who can change the measure? Keep one example of the decision the team revised and let the people affected describe the result. That gives a new employee something concrete to learn from, and a person outside the agency a reasonable way to judge whether the vision has influenced the service.
Development capability. Communicate and facilitate across difference.

pages.title: Making a decision when the cause is uncertain

spans.text: Direction and priorities     /     ARTICLE 36
Making a decision when the cause is uncertain

A supervisor asks for refresher training because several people received conflicting instructions. Training could help. It could also leave a careful employee following one of two contradictory instructions with greater confidence. The leader’s first responsibility is to define the difficulty precisely enough that the team can investigate it and decide how quickly somebody needs an answer.
Follow the work to the point where it diverges

Choose a recent example that can be discussed without identifying the person who sought help. Ask a worker from each team to demonstrate how they arrive at an answer. Look at the information available to them at that moment. Suppose both workers followed written guidance and the two documents give different directions. The team has found a cause that a reminder about diligence would leave untouched. If both documents agree, investigate other explanations, such as unclear exceptions or different information available on different shifts.

Agree on the consequence that matters. In this example, the person had to telephone twice and still did not know what to do next. Ask what already works in comparable cases. A colleague on another shift may know who resolves exceptions promptly. Sometimes making that route visible addresses the difficulty without creating a new project.
Make a proportionate decision and check the result

Identify who can issue an authoritative clarification. While that person resolves the discrepancy, a supervisor might arrange a common contact for cases in doubt and tell staff how to reach them. Give this interim decision an owner and an end date. Explain what is still uncertain so staff can answer questions accurately. If delay itself carries a cost, include that cost when weighing an interim arrangement against waiting for a permanent answer.

Once guidance is corrected, ask two people who were outside the working group to use it on the same situation. Compare the answers and see whether a caller would know the next step. Look again after a few weeks to see whether the conflict has returned. Tell the staff who first raised the concern what the organization changed and whether it helped.
Autocratic or directive leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
36    Making a decision when the cause is uncertain
Find out who carries the cost of an interim answer

Once two units discover their instructions conflict, agreeing that someone should fix the guidance is easy. The harder decision is what a person seeking help will experience until the correction is ready. One team may want to review all current cases immediately. The other has work due that day and can review only cases in which an unresolved question will cause a delay. A leader who tells both teams to make it their highest priority has assigned the same hours twice.

Open Resolving cross-unit priority conflicts and use the lesson on consequences and capacity. Set out what each team is trying to protect. Estimate how much time the review takes, which employees can do it and which work they would set aside. Compare two genuine alternatives. One might provide a named contact today for people facing an immediate consequence and schedule a broader review tomorrow. The other might assign a separate unit to help review, provided that unit has the knowledge and authority. A supervisor who favors either proposal should explain who will wait, for how long and what to do if circumstances change.
Distinguish a decision from a diagnosis

A directive response can be appropriate for the immediate instruction that everyone needs before a shift starts. It does little to explain why the conflict arose or why it escaped review. Delegate investigation to a person who can see how both instructions were revised and circulated. Equip them to talk with front-line staff who may have discovered the ambiguity earlier. Ask where they tried to send the question and what happened to it. An overlooked inbox, a copy saved on a shared drive and two owners who both expected the other to update the guidance call for different corrections.

Set a date for the two teams to test what changed. Give each the same unfamiliar example, ask them to show the source they used, and check what the person seeking help would hear. If both teams now give the same incorrect answer, consistency has improved while accuracy has not. Have the responsible program specialist judge the answer and a worker from outside the design group judge whether it can be put into practice. Those two checks give the leader a better basis for closing the issue.
Development capability. Examine assumptions and use evidence.

pages.title: Working with partners and the public

spans.text: Partners and communities     /     ARTICLE 37
Working with partners and the public

A community organization receives an invitation to “give feedback on service access.” Its staff have spent months telling agencies that many of their clients cannot answer a daytime call. Before accepting another invitation, they want to know which decision is open and whether anyone at the meeting can change it. A leader can answer those questions in the invitation itself. Doing so lets potential participants judge whether contributing is worth their time and what experience would be most useful.
Invite people into a decision they can influence

Suppose the decision concerns how a team offers callbacks. Explain what the team can change, what is fixed for now and when it will choose. Ask a question a person can answer from experience: “When we offered to call back, what made it possible or difficult for you to take that call?” Say how someone can respond, whom to contact for access needs and when contributors will hear back. An invitation that goes only to established partners can miss people who stopped trying to reach the program. Ask who else should have a way in.

Offer workable options such as a short phone conversation, a written response or a discussion through a trusted partner. Ask the partner what support participation would take. Avoid treating a partner’s perspective as a substitute for everyone it serves. Those who handle requests every day and those who have repeatedly missed a callback each know something the other may never see.
Show what happened to the input

When reviewing responses, keep differences visible. A scheduled call may work for someone who can reserve a lunch break. A person with an unpredictable shift may value an agreed alternative if the first call is missed. Counting which option received more mentions will not tell you how well either serves people in those circumstances.

Report the decision in language a contributor can recognize. Describe what you heard, what you will try, what you could not adopt and why. Give the change a review date and a person who can receive further concerns. When the pilot ends, ask whether people actually reached a worker. The people who gave the agency their time deserve to know what difference it made.
Democratic or participative leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
37    Working with partners and the public
Let a person change the design

A staff team draws two possible callback arrangements on paper. One offers a fixed appointment. The other offers an evening window. A participant who uses disability services says that neither solves the difficulty. The problem is that the phone displays an unfamiliar number, and they cannot tell a service call from an unwanted one. Their sister offers to take all the calls instead. The team now has three perspectives: the person’s experience, a family member’s useful offer and the agency’s concern about missed contacts. Each deserves attention. Only the person can tell the team which role they want their sister to have.

Work through Designing with people with disabilities and families. Use two simple versions of the proposed arrangement so participants can point to what they would keep, remove or replace. Ask the person how they want to be involved, whom they would like alongside them and what choice they would make if the team could change one more thing. Discuss a recognizable callback arrangement or a mutually agreed cue with the appropriate service owner. Leave room for the person to reject both initial proposals. Offering options matters only if the available choices can respond to what the person has said.
Make the limits of shared authority visible

Participative leadership works here when participants can influence the actual design. A leader can also delegate the choice of a pilot question to the people who will try it, with a clear account of constraints. Be careful with the phrase “the community agreed.” One person may prefer advance notice, another may need flexibility, and others may have had no opportunity to respond. Record which feedback led to which revision, where people differed and which decision remains with an authorized manager.

At the next meeting, bring the revised design and ask participants to use it in a realistic situation. Someone who can predict which call to answer has learned something about the new arrangement. The agency still needs experience from ordinary operation to decide whether it improves contact rates or reduces repeated work. Return a short account to participants in the formats they can use. That return lets them correct a mistaken interpretation before it becomes part of an agency decision.
Development capability. Communicate and facilitate across difference.

pages.title: Speaking to reporters on behalf of an agency

spans.text: Partners and communities     /     ARTICLE 38
Speaking to reporters on behalf of an agency

A local reporter calls late in the morning about residents who say they could not reach a program the day before. The reporter goes on air at noon. A staff member may know that their own phone was working, but that observation says little about the experience across the service. A useful first response is to capture the question, the affected time and place, the deadline and a way to get back in touch. Route the request to the designated spokesperson or communications team.
Prepare an answer that a resident can act on

If you have been assigned to speak, work with the people who can verify the facts. Find out which service was affected, what people should do now and which questions remain open. Agree on a time to provide an update. Acknowledge the request promptly, including when verification will take longer than the reporter’s deadline. A callback promise works only if someone has taken responsibility for making it.

For practice, imagine a voicemail queue failed on Tuesday morning. A program lead can verify the hours affected and that the queue is working again. They cannot yet say how many messages were lost. Construct a short response with those boundaries in place. Lead with the hours affected, give residents a verified way to reach the program and explain when you expect to know more about the messages. Avoid naming a cause while it is still under investigation.
Rehearse the difficult follow-up

Ask a colleague to play the reporter and press you on something you cannot confirm. Pause, answer the part you know and be direct about what you still need to check. If asked about an individual’s experience, stick to information you are authorized to share and explain how someone can seek help privately. An accurate response should still make sense if one sentence from it is broadcast alone.

Before the interview, say the essential information aloud at a conversational pace. Afterward, check that any promised information reached the reporter and that the service route you described remains usable. Respect for the reporter’s work and for residents’ time is visible in the accuracy of that follow-through.
Ethical leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
38    Speaking to reporters on behalf of an agency
Prepare for a question about unequal effects

Imagine that a reporter follows up on the missed messages. A partner says callers who needed an interpreter waited longer, and asks whether the department treated people differently. A spokesperson needs to take the concern seriously and describe the evidence accurately. One caller’s account can identify a failure the agency should examine. It does not establish how widespread the failure was. An overall average wait time cannot settle whether people experienced a consistent difference across languages.

In Communicating disparity findings with care, look at how to describe the measure and the limits of the comparison. Prepare a short working note with the date range, which contacts are included, what a wait measures and what happened to unreturned calls in the count. Ask a program colleague who knows the actual service how interpreter requests are recorded. If an unreturned message has no language information, the absence of a label may hide the people most affected. Make that limitation part of the analysis before the agency offers a public conclusion.
Use authority to make accuracy possible

An ethical approach makes clear which facts a spokesperson can verify now and what the agency is doing about the concern. A procedural approach ensures that the person authorized to share the information checks it, including the risk of identifying an individual through a very small group. An inclusive approach helps the team learn from people whose experience is missing from an internal dashboard. The public interview itself should leave people able to distinguish those three activities.

Rehearse a follow-up with a colleague. The reporter asks whether the figures disprove the partner’s account. Start with the finding you can support, explain in everyday terms which callers the figure leaves out, and give a realistic point of contact for an update. If people need assistance now, provide a verified route they can use. Have a second reader underline every statement that could be mistaken for a conclusion about why the problem occurred. Revise those sentences before the deadline. After the update, contact the relevant program owner about the practical question the reporting uncovered. A carefully worded answer earns its value when the agency also learns enough to improve what residents encounter.
Development capability. Examine assumptions and use evidence.

pages.contentsTitle: Being a Spokesperson and Interacting with Media

spans.text: Planning and delivery     /     ARTICLE 39
Workload prioritization

A phone number on a public referral page is wrong. A partner needs a decision about an event. A director has asked for presentation slides by Friday. All three requests have arrived before lunch. The order in which messages arrived tells you little about how long people can afford to wait. Prioritizing work requires a judgment about consequences. Someone needs to be able to explain that judgment to the people whose work will move.
Compare the consequences of waiting

Start with your role and the outcomes your team has agreed to deliver. Include routine service, commitments to partners, and time set aside to develop a skill. An inventory helps you see an important piece of work that nobody is emailing about. For each item, identify who needs the result, the earliest step someone else is waiting for, and the deadline you can confirm. Ask the requester where a date came from. A presentation due Friday may be needed in accessible form on Wednesday.

Consider impact and effort together. Correcting the phone number could take ten minutes and spare callers repeated failed attempts. Replacing an entire directory could benefit many more people and require several weeks. Give the correction immediate attention and reserve time for the larger repair. A small formatting preference can wait for a scheduled update. A laborious redesign that serves no identified need deserves a conversation before anyone starts it. A fixed service obligation still needs time even when it scores poorly on a convenience measure.
Make the choice visible

Check your order with the people who depend on it. You may learn that the partner only needs a room capacity today and can wait for the complete agenda. Offer that smaller decision, identify who will confirm it, and tell the director when the slides will be ready. When tradeoffs are close, agree on criteria such as service impact, timing, and the number of teams waiting. Give the most important criterion greater weight and discuss any ranking that surprises the group.

Put the first action on your calendar and contact the person authorized to correct the number. Reserve the next block of time for the directory. At your next check-in, ask which consequence you anticipated correctly and what new information changed the order. A useful priority decision gives colleagues enough notice to change their own plans.
Autocratic or directive leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
39    Workload prioritization
When a quick repair competes with a lasting improvement

Correcting the referral number solves today's error. A colleague discovers that three units maintain their own copies of the same contact list. Correcting every copy will take an afternoon. Establishing a reliable owner and a way to tell partners about changes will take a month. Give those two pieces of work separate places in the plan. Otherwise the quick correction may be reported as a permanent solution, or the search for a permanent solution may leave a wrong number on the page for another week.

An impact and effort grid helps separate readily achievable changes, substantial investments, convenient low-value tasks and work that consumes considerable effort for little return. Decide whose effort counts. One hour saved at the central office may cost twenty partner sites an hour each. Before rating the benefit, ask who uses the number, what happens after a failed call and whether there is another usable way to reach the service. Staff do not need to know a caller's identity to find out whether the published route works.

For a closer choice, agree on criteria and weights before rating the proposals. If preventing interruption to a public service counts twice as much as convenience for staff, write that down. Try the ranking again with a smaller weight. If the first and second choices switch places, explain the disputed judgment to the person with authority to decide. A weighted matrix is especially valuable when it reveals why two reasonable people disagree.
Choose when to direct and when to invite judgment

Compare Autocratic or directive leadership with Democratic or participative leadership in the leadership styles collection. Have two colleagues rehearse the opening minute after the error is discovered. The first assigns a person to correct the number immediately and names who will verify it. The second asks partner offices how numbers are kept current and which notification method they already use. The first response suits an immediate correction. The second gives people who maintain the network a say in how it will work. Using either approach throughout would leave part of the problem unsolved.

Reserve time for the longer repair alongside development commitments and recurring work. Agree on a review date with the person whose presentation was delayed. The first action can be as short as opening each public listing and recording where the number appears. Once repairs are in place, ask a colleague outside the team to follow the route. Look at what the caller can now do and whether the team can explain who will catch the next change.
Development capability. Connect equity with workforce decisions.
Planning and delivery     /     ARTICLE 40
Why plan your workload?

A calendar can show a full week of appointments while hiding the work each appointment creates. A one-hour community conversation may require two hours to prepare, another to arrange access, and several more to verify and report what people said. A workload plan puts that labor in view early enough for a supervisor and employee to make different commitments.
Draw a picture of the next few weeks

Choose a period long enough to see a collision coming. Start with three two-week columns on paper or in a spreadsheet. Give each major responsibility a row. Include everyday service, project work, preparation, follow-up, staff development, and planned time away. Keep the categories broad enough that maintaining the plan takes only a few minutes. If hours are difficult to estimate, shade a small, medium, or large share of each period. Use a label as well as shading so another reader can interpret the estimate.

Suppose an analyst has 64 hours available in the next period after planned leave. Routine requests typically take 32 hours. Preparing a partner workshop takes 18. The analyst expects to spend 16 hours on a report and four coaching a new colleague. The plan calls for 70 hours. A six-hour gap can look manageable until an unexpected service question consumes the only unscheduled afternoon. Ask which estimate is most uncertain and what the people doing the work have learned from a similar period.
Use the plan to change a commitment

The supervisor can ask the workshop owner whether someone else can prepare the materials, or whether the report reader needs the whole report at once. If the analyst can deliver validated figures this week and commentary next week, check that the later period has room and notify the reader. Protecting coaching time also has a work consequence. The new colleague may take on part of the next report once they have practiced with support.

Use the next check-in to compare estimated and actual effort. If routine requests took 40 hours, revise that row and discuss the continuing effect. A useful plan allows both people to see who authorized a change, when relief will arrive, and whether moving work has simply created a new peak two weeks later.
Bureaucratic or procedural leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
40    Why plan your workload?
Separate work time from waiting time

A meeting with community advisers may need a month of lead time even if its organizer spends only three days working on it. Someone must confirm a date, arrange communication supports, send material early enough for advisers to review it, and allow contributors to correct the record. These activities do different things to the plan. Reserving a room consumes little staff time but may control the date of everything else. Reviewing responses takes longer and may be possible while the team waits for confirmations.

On a copy of the plan, mark the earliest date each task can start, the person or response it depends on and the latest useful completion date. Ask people who usually do the work to review the estimates. Include regular supervision, required learning and recurring office coverage. If a bilingual colleague has been helping staff navigate questions about access arrangements, find out what that support takes. Make responsibility explicit and arrange appropriate language services where needed. Unassigned work is easily mistaken for spare capacity.

Use Make participation more accessible to examine the event before promising an attendance date. Its questions about preparing multiple ways to contribute can uncover tasks the plan missed. For an evening gathering, for instance, someone needs to receive daytime written comments, bring them into the discussion and get back to the contributors. Put that time and an owner in the plan. Someone checking the calendar should be able to see which part could move and what people would lose if it did.
Plan for a disruption before it happens

Rehearse two versions of the week. In one, both staff responsible for arranging the session are available. In the other, one covers an unplanned vacancy. What can a backup take over with the information already available? Which choice needs a manager? Shared or distributed leadership can give a second employee authority to make routine arrangements. That authority needs to exist before a rushed handoff. A colleague who knows the history but cannot confirm a booking can only report what is about to go wrong.

At the next check-in, compare the forecast with the work actually done by category. A single unexpected absence is poor grounds for a permanent redesign. Repeated weeks in which access preparation or community follow-up has to happen after hours point to a problem in the allocation itself. Change the estimate, assign coverage or reduce the volume promised. Tell the people expecting the work which decision was made and when they can rely on the revised plan.
Development capability. Share knowledge and build future capability.
