pages.title: Asking leadership for a workable plan

spans.text: Planning and delivery     /     ARTICLE 41
Asking leadership for a workable plan

“When another urgent request comes in, which commitment should I move?” is a question an employee can reasonably put to a supervisor. It asks the person who can set priorities to make a decision. This matters when different managers have each approved work without seeing their combined effect on the people carrying it out.
Show the pattern and its cost

Look back over a representative stretch of work. Record what was assigned, what changed, where time went, and who experienced a delay. Include repetitive work, hours beyond the usual schedule, and previous attempts to simplify the process. One unusually busy day may call for short-term help. The same clash every reporting cycle calls for a decision about ownership, staffing, or scope. Use examples that describe the work without disclosing private information about people served.

Imagine a specialist who covers a public inbox and prepares a recurring partner briefing. On three successive briefing days, two teams independently requested the same figures in different formats. The specialist prepared both and left inbox coverage to a colleague who had not been told to expect it. Each manager saw a report arrive on time. Neither could see the colleague’s interrupted work or the time spent reconciling two versions.
Ask for a decision someone can carry out

Bring a recommendation and a real alternative. “I can prepare one set of figures for both teams if they agree on the definitions by Tuesday. If both versions are essential, I need someone assigned to the inbox on briefing mornings. Which can we arrange?” Ask what constraint you might be missing. One audience may genuinely need a different reporting period. The supervisor can negotiate that distinction while the specialist estimates the additional work.

Write down the decision, the person who will speak with the other managers, and the date you will see whether it helped. If nothing changes, bring the specific unresolved commitment back before its next deadline. Explain what fits within your available hours and what still needs a decision. If an ongoing problem persists, a mentor, another appropriate leader, or Human Resources can help identify how to raise it. The employee can describe the collision. Management has to decide how the organization will absorb it.
Democratic or participative leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
41    Asking leadership for a workable plan
Make conflicting assignments visible without putting colleagues on trial

An employee can bring a real constraint into the room without disclosing personal information about the people served. Prepare a short account of the competing work. For each commitment, identify who authorized it, the latest useful date, what has already been done and the consequence of delay. Include unplanned tasks that arrived during the last comparable period. Repeated requests for help may explain why an assignment that takes four uninterrupted hours has stayed open for a week.

At the meeting, show the supervisor two achievable sequences. For example, an analyst could deliver an estimate before a partner's budget meeting and defer formatting a dashboard, or complete the dashboard first and give the partner a date for validated numbers. A third option might be to send an unverified estimate. Explain what someone could wrongly commit to if they mistook that number for a verified one. The supervisor can now weigh a scheduling cost against an information risk. A worker should not have to settle that tradeoff simply by responding to the loudest request.

If the direction is “both by Friday,” ask what support or change in scope makes that feasible. Perhaps the dashboard can use an existing layout and the estimate needs a second analyst's review. Identify both contributors and make sure they know the assignment has changed. After the conversation, tell each requester what will arrive and when. That also gives a supervisor the chance to correct a misunderstanding before other people build their plans around it.
Practice what happens when the answer does not resolve the issue

Use Leadership style scenarios with a supervisor or peer. The pathway asks learners to evaluate responses to situations where people hold different amounts of authority. Apply that reasoning to workload. One person plays a manager who controls the deadline. The other plays the only analyst who knows the validation step. Repeat the exchange with the manager taking a coaching approach, drawing out estimates and alternatives, then taking a directive approach to choosing the order once those facts are clear.

Look for two things in the response. Can the employee raise a material concern without being treated as uncooperative? Can both people state who decided and who will inform the other manager? If the manager declines to choose and deadlines remain incompatible, send a brief account of the remaining decision through the ordinary management channel. State the earliest time a choice would prevent harm. Where the pattern persists, a higher-level scheduling discussion or advice from an appropriate workplace resource may help clarify who can resolve it.
Development capability. Communicate and facilitate across difference.

pages.title: Managing a project from assignment to handoff

spans.text: Planning and delivery     /     ARTICLE 42
Managing a project from assignment to handoff

Suppose a program team has promised to revise an appointment letter for a pilot with two partner offices. One colleague knows the service rules, another writes in plain language, and a third coordinates release. Each understands a different piece of the work. The project manager gives them a shared definition of a finished letter and a way to make decisions when time, cost, and quality pull in different directions.
Define what finished means

Agree with the sponsor on the people who will use the letter, the problem it should solve, and the scope of the pilot. For example, readers should be able to identify the appointment date, arrange a change, and find help in a format they can use. Identify who can approve the wording and who will authorize distribution. A team can complete a beautiful draft and still miss its deadline if no one has secured a decision from the person who owns the outgoing communication.

Work backward from the first mailing. A printer needs a release file. The release file depends on accessible formatting and a final review. Testing a draft with readers can expose confusing instructions early enough to change them. Ask each contributor what they need from the previous person and when. Estimate the staff time involved, including what other work someone would give up to accelerate a review.
Bring the sponsor an actual choice

Halfway through the pilot, a partner asks to add a second letter type. The project manager can describe how much design and testing that adds and put alternatives before the sponsor. Keep the agreed mailing date for the first letter and schedule the second, or extend the pilot with both offices’ agreement. Record who chose the option and who needs to hear about it. A short check-in focused on outstanding decisions can be more useful than another meeting where everyone recounts their week.

At handoff, have someone who did not write the letter locate the approved version and explain how a later correction would reach both offices. Give the person maintaining it the decision history, the open questions, and a date for reviewing early feedback. That last exchange turns a temporary project into a piece of work people can sustain.
Empowering or delegative leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
42    Managing a project from assignment to handoff
A late request changes more than the schedule

Halfway through the letter pilot, a partner asks the project manager to add instructions for appealing a decision. Residents have been asking about that process, and the request deserves attention. It may also change who must review the content, which versions need revision and whether people receiving the letter will understand what it means. An enthusiastic promise at a progress meeting could commit the team to releasing material it has had no opportunity to verify.

Write a short change proposal. Describe the difficulty the partner reported, the proposed addition, who would need to verify it and the effect on the planned pilot. Compare adding the information now, directing readers to a verified contact for the moment or treating the issue as separate work with its own responsible owner. Ask a colleague who knows the distinction between an appointment message and a decision notice to review the options. The project sponsor can then decide what belongs in this release and communicate how the other need will be addressed.

The One DHS area Planning and delivery includes project management and financial stewardship. Staff hours, partner review and the time needed to correct a faulty mailing all belong in the cost discussion. A decision to keep the date may be defensible if the team narrows the pilot. To release the same quantity by the same date while quietly removing an agreed access check would change the promised quality. Bring that tradeoff to the sponsor in words the people doing the checking would recognize.
Test the handoff from the receiving office

In Make a process easier to use, start with the task a resident should be able to complete when the letter arrives. Give a colleague unfamiliar with the project the reviewed version and a realistic situation. For example, the time offered conflicts with a medical appointment. Ask the colleague to find out how to request another time and what happens if the first contact does not answer. If the letter requires a phone call, ask the receiving office what instructions it gives at that point.

Use the answers to trace a failure to the right owner. If the letter points to the wrong location, the document owner can correct it. If the instructions point to an unanswered line, a wording change alone will not resolve the difficulty. Record the remaining issue with the person authorized to handle it. Close the pilot when the receiving team can identify the approved version, the person who maintains it and the route for reporting a new problem after the project manager moves on.
Development capability. Share knowledge and build future capability.

pages.title: Evaluating a program while there is still time to change it

spans.text: Planning and delivery     /     ARTICLE 43
Evaluating a program while there is still time to change it

A pilot offers evening callbacks to people who cannot speak with program staff during the day. After the first month, the team reports that it completed 60 calls. A leader considering a second shift needs to know more. How many people wanted an evening call? Could they actually reach someone who could help? Did evening coverage reduce the time others could reach staff during the day? Each question points to a different piece of evidence and a different decision.
Start with the decision the evidence will support

Before the pilot, write down the change people should experience. In this example, a useful outcome is that people who request an evening conversation can complete their next step. The number of calls placed describes staff activity. The share of people reached among those requesting a call describes access to the conversation. The share who could act afterward tells the team something about its usefulness. Decide who can collect each measure, when to collect it, and how to protect the people behind the numbers.

Capture a starting point where one exists, such as the typical time from a request to a successful contact under the earlier schedule. Agree on how to handle repeated attempts so that one person called four times does not count as four people served. If the pilot is already running, use available records and identify the gaps. Interviews and a small review of participants’ experiences can reveal where a process succeeds or breaks down, even when earlier figures are incomplete.
Let people help interpret the finding

Suppose many evening callers are reached but few complete the next step. Ask participants and staff to describe what happened after the call. A required handoff might be available only during business hours. Invite people to discuss unexpected effects as well. A conversation at an existing community gathering or a map of effects drawn by participants can reveal consequences a fixed survey missed. People who never reached the program may need a different way to contribute.

Use what you learn during the pilot. Try an agreed handoff on one evening shift, track what happens, and report whose experience is still missing. A change over time may have several explanations. Tell the decision maker what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain, and what would justify expanding, revising, or ending the pilot.
Transformative or equity-centered leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
43    Evaluating a program while there is still time to change it
Give the count a denominator and an honest interpretation

Sixty completed calls could mean sixty residents reached once, thirty reached twice, or a mix of completed conversations and voicemails. Define a successful contact and the unit being counted before comparing shifts. Suppose 80 distinct people requested an evening callback during a pilot week. Staff reached 48 of them within the agreed window. The reach rate among people requesting that option is 60 percent. It says nothing by itself about people who needed the option and never learned it existed. A different question needs a different population.

Use Plan how to learn from results to specify the population, calculation, baseline, source of evidence and who can authorize its use. Decide what the team will do if a signal changes. If fewer people can get through during the day, the staffing pattern may need to change even if evening contacts rise. If people can answer evening calls but still have to start over the next morning, ask whether evening staff have access to the help callers actually need. Avoid collecting names in an evaluation worksheet. Where subgroup comparisons are appropriate, work with the data owner on reporting safeguards.

Build the baseline prospectively if you can. If the pilot already began, examine which comparable records exist and document any changes in definitions. An unusually busy week, a new notice or staff vacancies could account for part of a difference. Showing what happened and deciding what to try next can be worthwhile even when a causal conclusion would outrun the evidence.
Invite people to make sense of an unexpected result

Numbers rarely explain why an option was usable. A program evaluator might join an existing partner meeting, conduct interviews or invite participants to map effects that appeared after the pilot. In a ripple effects exercise, a participant could describe being able to handle a call outside work. Another may describe a later disruption because the promised time was too vague. Trace those experiences back to a feature the team could change. Seek differing experiences, including from people whose calls were missed.

Bring a preliminary interpretation back to the people who helped produce it. Ask what the team has overlooked and who is absent from the account. Working this way while a service is still changing is a form of developmental evaluation. Record a decision such as narrowing the callback window for one week, the workload consequence to monitor and the evidence that would justify extending the change. The leader who authorized the pilot should be able to explain why the decision serves the public and what uncertainty remains.
Development capability. Examine assumptions and use evidence.

pages.title: Making better use of workplace technology

spans.text: Planning and delivery     /     ARTICLE 44
Making better use of workplace technology

Two people can spend an afternoon correcting the same guidance and end up with two incompatible files. A faster application will do little for them until the team agrees where the working copy lives and how a colleague can recognize the approved version. Technology is most useful when staff can name a task it should make easier and check whether the person doing the task experienced an improvement.
Follow one piece of work

Trace a common activity from request through completion. Suppose county partners submit questions ahead of an office hour. Staff copy questions out of email, group similar ones, assign speakers, and circulate revised agendas. Ask the coordinator to show where information gets retyped, where an edit gets lost, and which decisions still need a person who understands the issue. Look at features in tools already available to the team. A shared list with a topic, owner, status, and due date might resolve more of the problem than buying a new system.

Try the smallest change with a few colleagues. Give them the link from the invitation and ask them to find their assignments and update them. Include someone joining remotely and someone who navigates by keyboard. Check which information belongs in the shared space, who can view it, and who can change it. Keep identifying service details out of a general agenda. Pair a calendar reminder with a named reviewer so an automated notice does not become a substitute for a decision.
Teach the task and examine the result

Have a colleague demonstrate how to enter a new question and find its answer. Then let another employee do it with realistic sample information. Offer short written instructions and a contact for help. Someone who uses the software daily may still need support when an update moves a familiar control. Give that colleague a useful problem to solve while practicing.

After two meetings, compare the effort to prepare the agenda and the number of questions left without an owner. Ask partners whether they can still submit a question through an accessible channel, including when their organization cannot open the shared workspace. If work merely moved from the coordinator to dozens of partners, revise the process. The measure of success is how well the whole exchange works.
Adaptive and situational leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
44    Making better use of workplace technology
Design a workflow that survives a lost connection

To evaluate a technology choice, carry one task across offices with different working conditions. Suppose a county partner is revising a public information sheet with a DHS colleague. The partner has intermittent access to the shared workspace. The DHS editor needs the latest approved guidance and the communications reviewer needs a clean copy for publication. Agree on what the reviewers will treat as the active draft, who may change it and how someone can contribute when the shared session is unavailable.

Walk through an outage. The partner submits a correction by an approved alternative route while another editor revises the same paragraph. Who resolves the conflict? Where will the decision be recorded? Is there a way for the partner to see whether the correction survived? An agreed file name is helpful. An identified owner with enough time to review the change is more important. Automating distribution before the team has settled those questions can spread an outdated version more quickly to everyone using it.

Connect this exercise to Digital access in the One DHS competency collection and to the Plain language and accessible documents checklist. Have an employee unfamiliar with the draft try to locate the current heading, the link destination and the next action using the method they ordinarily use. Observe what happens when a digital copy becomes a printout or a downloaded PDF. If a change is visible only through colored markup, publishing the file in another format may remove its meaning.
Teach one feature well enough for someone else to take over

Select a feature that addresses a documented difficulty. It might be version history for two people editing at different times, or a reminder for the person responsible for checking an expiring contact. An experienced user can demonstrate the feature on a practice document and then hand control to a colleague. Ask the colleague to restore a prior wording, identify the person responsible for approval and prepare the clean version. The colleague's ability to carry out the task is more informative than a demonstration led entirely by an expert.

Compare the revised workflow with the earlier one over a small number of routine changes. Count interruptions, duplicate requests and corrections made after release. Ask whether anyone now spends extra time converting a file or transcribing comments. If the burden has moved to a partner with less technical support, revisit the tool or permission settings with the appropriate owner. Retain the technique when the work is easier to complete across the whole route and the team can sustain it after the person who introduced it is away.
Development capability. Build inclusion and accessibility into work.

pages.title: Writing a grant proposal a reviewer can use

spans.text: Planning and delivery     /     ARTICLE 45
Writing a grant proposal a reviewer can use

A convincing proposal lets a reviewer trace a line from a documented need to an activity, a budget, and a result that people can recognize. Clarity about that line also protects the people who might have to deliver the work. A promise that reads well in an application can become a difficult commitment when a partner has neither agreed to it nor been budgeted to carry it out.
Decide whether the opportunity fits

Read the funding notice before drafting the story. Identify who may apply, what costs and activities are eligible, the period of work, required attachments, any match, submission instructions, and the selection criteria. Assign someone to resolve uncertainties early. If the funder limits eligibility to community organizations, a state team cannot assume it can lead an application. Ask the potential partner what role, if any, it wants and check what the notice permits.

Imagine an opportunity to improve residents’ access to service information. A community partner proposes evening sessions where people can try finding an answer and ask questions as they go. Learn what the funder means by improved access and what the partner has already heard from residents. Verify that the proposed session time, language support, and follow-up make sense to the intended participants. A funder’s interest and an agency’s favorite project may overlap only partly.
Build one account of the work

Describe the barrier precisely. Explain who will prepare materials, host sessions, respond to questions, and determine whether people found what they needed. Connect each activity to a supportable cost. If the narrative promises interpretation at four events but the budget pays for two, the reader has uncovered a service decision the partners still need to make. Agree on the scope and reflect it consistently in the work plan, budget, and narrative.

Keep one file set with named owners and due dates for approvals and partner contributions. Before submitting, ask someone outside the drafting team to score the application against the notice. Have them point to the evidence for each criterion and explain, in their own words, what would change for a resident. A gap in that explanation tells you which part of the proposal still needs work while there is time to fix it.
Bureaucratic or procedural leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
45    Writing a grant proposal a reviewer can use
Read the proposal once as the funder and once as the partner

A proposal for community navigation can be convincing on its first reading and unworkable on its second. From the funder's perspective, the narrative connects residents to services and the budget pays for a navigator. From a partner's perspective, a navigator is also expected to organize meetings, arrange interpretation, make referrals, answer after-hours calls and document what happened. Determine whether those responsibilities can be delivered by the position and hours the budget describes. Ask the partner privately which promises it has the people and resources to make.

Give each requirement a place in the application. For a requirement to demonstrate community involvement, identify the work done with people affected and the choices their input actually influenced. A supportive remark at an event does not establish that an organization has agreed to recruit participants or share information. Obtain a partner's agreement to the specific role and wording before counting that contribution. If the funder's priorities and the proposed service diverge, discuss whether a different opportunity would fit better before rewriting the project to appeal to a reviewer.

In the One DHS curriculum, the finance and contracts cultural humility simulation examines applicant questions, review against published criteria and concerns after an award. Work through the applicant question from the other side of the desk. Which application requirement would a small community organization need the most time to understand? Where could an official clarification help every applicant? Bring a question through the funder's stated process. Preserve any official answer and review the draft against it.
Give the reviewer a traceable claim

Take one sentence, such as a promise to help residents complete a referral. Name the obstacle the team has observed and how it learned about it. Describe which activity the funds would support, which role would perform it and what evidence could show whether residents completed the next step. Separate the output the applicant controls, such as offering navigation appointments, from the benefit it hopes will follow. A partner's waitlist can affect whether someone receives a service even after a successful referral.

Ask a fresh reader to trace that sentence to the budget and timetable. A translation commitment should have time for review and a realistic cost. A quarterly report should have an owner and an agreed source for its figures. If any link fails, repair the work plan as well as the prose. Before submission, use a single filed version and a record of approvals, so the people preparing to deliver a successful award can see precisely what was promised.
Development capability. Build inclusion and accessibility into work.

spans.text: Planning and delivery     /     ARTICLE 46
Communicating clearly when you delegate

“Please coordinate the listening session” can mean booking a room to one person and designing the entire engagement to another. A supervisor who discovers the difference on the morning of the session has left an important decision unmade. Good delegation gives a colleague a result to own, the authority and resources to reach it, and a clear way to surface a problem before it lands on participants.
Agree on the result and the decisions

Start with the purpose. Suppose a team wants people receiving services to help it choose which parts of an orientation need revision. Ask the colleague leading the session how they would gather views, whose perspective the plan might miss, and what support they need. Agree on the date, what participants should be able to influence, and how their input will get back to the person deciding. Define what a usable handoff looks like. A short account of competing priorities and unanswered questions may serve the team better than a page of attendance figures.

Match the assignment to the person’s experience and authority. A first-time facilitator might design the questions and lead a small discussion with an experienced colleague available. The supervisor may need to approve spending or make introductions to partners. Let the facilitator choose a workable method within those boundaries. If the supervisor prescribes every question and rejects every change, accountability for the session design still rests with the supervisor.
Stay available at the moments that matter

Set a checkpoint when the colleague has a draft invitation and there is still time to change the plan. A shared document, an agreed response time, and an accessible meeting option help people working from different locations contribute. Invite written suggestions before the checkpoint. Name who resolves a disagreement if the group cannot. For a larger effort, record owners and dates in one place everyone involved can use.

Have the colleague explain what they will decide and what would prompt them to call you. Afterward, review an actual moment from the session together. Did participants understand the decision? What helped someone raise a different view? Recognize the colleague’s judgment, ask what responsibility they want next, and carry out the commitments only you have authority to make.

Before handing over an assignment, name any prescribed procedure, accessibility requirement or approval that limits how the employee can do it. Within those limits, give them room to choose a method and explain how the result will be judged. Holding someone responsible for the outcome while privately dictating every choice makes it difficult to tell whose judgment is being developed.
Empowering or delegative leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
46    Communicating clearly when you delegate
How much authority does the employee actually have

A manager delegates a listening session to a colleague who has organized several internal meetings. The colleague can reserve a room but cannot authorize overtime, change a program deadline or promise that a public recommendation will be adopted. Participants may ask about all three. Agree beforehand on the language the facilitator can use to explain who holds each decision and when a response can be expected. Give the facilitator access to the responsible people, including a backup when the sponsor is unavailable.

Work with the Empowering or delegative leadership lesson. Pick one decision to transfer completely, one the facilitator can make after consultation and one the sponsor must retain. For example, the facilitator can choose how people offer comments, consult an access specialist about the format and refer a budget request to the sponsor. Consider what happens if a participant needs more time and the room reservation ends at four. A staff member with authority to open a written response period can act immediately. A staff member who has to seek approval needs a name and a response time.

Visibility complicates a first assignment. A person can learn a public-facing task without having to manage every difficult exchange alone. Offer a rehearsal with a colleague playing an impatient partner. Let the employee answer, then ask what information or authority would have helped them answer more accurately. Decide in advance when the sponsor will step in and how they will return the floor. An intervention that rescues a capable employee at every hesitation can deprive the person of the very opportunity the assignment was meant to provide.
Set up a record people in different places can use

When a distributed team is preparing the session, a meeting, a chat and a shared document may each hold a different answer. Agree on one current record of the objective, authorized decisions, due dates and unresolved questions. Give staff a way to flag a question between meetings. Use check-ins for decisions that benefit from discussion and return the decision to the shared record so it reaches people who were away.

After the session, compare the delegated objective with what participants experienced. Did people know which decisions they could affect? Did the facilitator receive useful feedback and get credit for their work? Did the sponsor follow up on questions the facilitator was asked to refer? Use the answers to decide which responsibility the employee is prepared to take on next. Assigning someone a visible task builds capability when the experience includes authority, preparation and a fair account of the result.
Development capability. Communicate and facilitate across difference.
Fair access and inclusion     /     ARTICLE 47
Cultural awareness, competence and humility

A supervisor notices that the people who stay after a meeting often shape the decision. Everyone had a chance to speak during the meeting, and the supervisor assumed that settled the question. Looking again, she realizes the team treats staying late, thinking aloud, and disagreeing on the spot as signs of engagement. People have many reasons for choosing a different way to contribute. The supervisor’s own expectations are the part she can examine first.
Recognize the expectation, then change a practice

Cultural awareness includes recognizing the habits you bring to a situation and how much influence those habits carry in your role. Write down the observation before you interpret it. “Three people sent comments the next morning” gives you something to examine. Calling those employees indecisive tells you more about the standard you have applied. Ask how people would like to contribute and when they need to see materials to give a considered response. A cultural brief can help a leader formulate a question. The person involved can answer for their own circumstances.

Competence develops as you use what you learn. If the supervisor needs feedback on a proposal, she can distribute it in advance, invite disagreement through several channels, and name the time when the decision will close. She can use the same reasoning in a service review by asking community partners which choices are still open and which arrangements would make participation possible. Formal learning can deepen the work. A qualified administrator can help a leader use the Intercultural Development Inventory to choose a development goal. Tribal-state relations learning can prepare staff to recognize a distinct government-to-government relationship in work involving Tribal Nations.
Remain answerable to the people affected

Humility matters when someone tells you the change missed the point. Perhaps staff could send a note but decisions still followed the private conversation afterward. The supervisor can acknowledge what she allowed to happen, reopen a decision where feasible, and put the actual reasons for the next decision where the team can examine them. Ask the employees who raised the concern how the new arrangement worked, without asking any one person to speak for a whole community. Over time, their ability to influence the work is a better guide to progress than the supervisor’s confidence in her own cultural knowledge.
Adaptive and situational leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
47    Cultural awareness, competence and humility
Examine the demand the institution places on a person

It helps to examine whose account becomes part of a public decision. Consider a person who wants help staying near family. A staff member asks about independent living goals and records that the person has no interest in becoming more independent. The wording has shifted the meaning. The person described a relationship they want to maintain. The record interprets their preference through the staff member's idea of growth.

Several explanations remain open. The person may want more control over daily decisions while sharing a home. They may want a different arrangement and fear losing support. They may be satisfied with the current arrangement. A question that opens those possibilities is, “Which decisions about home do you want to make yourself, and whom do you want involved?” Give time for a response using the person's chosen way to communicate. With permission, include the people they identify. Keep their choices distinguishable from the worker's interpretation and from relatives' preferences.

Read the chapter Learning about communities without predicting people alongside a community brief that relates to a specific service question. Identify an assumption the reading helps you recognize in your own practice. Use it to prepare a better question for the next interaction. Because a community account can describe a historical relationship with public institutions, it may help explain why a staff practice deserves scrutiny. It cannot establish what a particular individual has experienced or what they want.
Move from personal learning to an organizational response

Suppose a supervisor finds that several workers use the same independence question because it is the only example used in orientation. Coaching one employee can repair one encounter. The wider issue belongs to whoever maintains orientation and the planning process. Ask a small group, including people with experience of receiving support, to draft other ways to invite discussion of control, support and belonging. Show how a worker could document each preference faithfully within the current process and who can consider a change to the materials.

Cultural humility is visible in what happens after someone challenges the revised examples. A suggestion may still assume that everyone wants relatives involved. Rework it so the person can choose privacy as readily as support. Ask participants to review the wording and say what a worker would actually do differently. Revisit a small sample of practice situations after the change. Look for faithful accounts of varied choices and a clear next action the person could recognize as their own.
Development capability. Examine your own cultural default.

resources: Learning about communities without predicting people

spans.text: Fair access and inclusion     /     ARTICLE 48
Accessibility in documents and meetings

A resident opens an invitation to a public session. The address appears in a picture of a flyer. The registration link says “here,” and the sentence about accommodations is also part of the picture. A colleague can read everything on the screen and still miss the problem. Someone using a screen reader may have no practical way to find the address, distinguish the link, or learn whom to contact. The author can fix those barriers before the invitation goes out.
Publish information people can act on

Begin with an accessible document template. Give the meeting a descriptive title, use built-in heading styles for sections, and put the date, time, location, and contact in ordinary text. Give a link a name that describes the action it opens. If an image conveys information, provide a text equivalent that communicates what someone needs to know. Use sufficient contrast, and label the choices in words. A calendar marked only with red and green dots leaves the meaning uncertain even if someone can distinguish the colors.

Run the accessibility checker and examine what it flags. Then try a practical task. Starting at the top, can you navigate by keyboard to the accommodation contact? If you read only the headings and links, can you identify how to register? A tool may confirm that an image has alternative text even when its description says only “graphic.” The author still has to decide whether the information makes sense.
Carry access through the event

Include the appropriate contact for accommodation requests and an accessible way to reach them. Choose a meeting platform that supports captions and plan for any requested communication support with the people coordinating it. Provide materials in advance where possible. During a presentation, describe the trend in a chart aloud and include the figures in accessible text. Give someone joining by phone a way to participate in an exercise that others complete in chat.

Before the session, assign someone to monitor access problems and respond privately when appropriate. If the captions fail, pause so the affected participant can help identify a workable option. Afterward, ask whether people could find the materials, contribute, and receive follow-up in a usable form. Keep improvements in the template so the next organizer starts with what the team learned.
Inclusive leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
48    Accessibility in documents and meetings
Rehearse the route from invitation to participation

Open Make participation more accessible and follow the experience of a resident who receives the digital invitation and calls to arrange participation. Start with the contact details. Does the invitation name the person or office that receives requests? Can someone use more than one channel if the first is difficult? Does the person answering know who arranges the support and when to respond? A well-formatted invitation can still leave a resident unable to join a conversation when the next person in the chain has no instructions.

In a rehearsal, give different participants a task rather than asking for a general opinion. One person finds the location and asks how to contribute in writing. Another joins online and locates caption controls. A facilitator explains a chart aloud in enough detail for someone to take part in the decision about it. A note-taker records a written contribution alongside one offered verbally. If a question is put to a vote, check whether all offered participation methods allow a person to weigh in before the decision closes.

The Plain language and accessible documents checklist can guide the material review. Use native headings for structure, meaningful link text, a usable reading order and sufficient contrast. Where colors identify status or options, put the meaning in words as well. Run the built-in accessibility checker and review the flags. Then use the document to perform a real task. Software can detect certain missing elements and still be unable to tell whether an image description explains the information a reader needs.
Give someone the authority to repair the meeting

Suppose captions fail midway through the discussion. Decide in advance who can pause the meeting, arrange another way to participate and determine whether a decision needs to wait. A directive response can be appropriate when the immediate action is clear. State what is happening, take responsibility for the adjustment and explain when business will resume. Ask the participant privately what would make participation possible. They should have a choice about what to share in front of the group.

The later review belongs to the team that organized the session. Did staff know how to reach support? Did people get a chance to revisit information they missed? Was feedback through a later channel considered before the decision? Choose a repair that addresses the gap found in the rehearsal or event. A reusable meeting template can carry the corrected contact information and decision procedure into the next session. Review it again when the technology, venue or audience changes.
Development capability. Build inclusion and accessibility into work.

spans.text: Fair access and inclusion     /     ARTICLE 49
Practicing allyship where you have influence

A unit selects people for temporary project lead assignments through informal recommendations. The assignments build the experience supervisors look for in later selection decisions. An employee points out that the same small circle keeps hearing about them first. The manager who receives that concern has standing to ask how assignments are made. That standing gives her a way to act even though the existing arrangement has worked well for her personally.
Examine who can enter and who sets the rules

Look at how someone actually becomes a candidate. Who hears about the work? Who can put a name forward? What counts as evidence that a person can lead? Which staff have previously been given a chance to produce that evidence? A criterion that sounds reasonable can keep rewarding earlier access. Ask how exceptions are granted, who can challenge a decision, and whether people face different consequences for doing so. A pattern deserves examination even when nobody has made an openly exclusionary remark.

Speak with the person who raised the concern about what support would be useful and what they want kept private. They may want to present the issue themselves, ask for an introduction, or prefer that management examine its own procedures without identifying them. Take responsibility for finding information you can obtain yourself. A colleague should be able to raise a barrier without becoming the unpaid coordinator of the entire response.
Use your authority and account for the result

The manager could bring the assignment process to the group that controls it, propose publishing the duties and selection criteria, and arrange coverage so interested staff can take part. If a colleague has developed a workable approach and wants to present it, introduce them as its author and make room for them to answer questions. The manager can handle objections about staffing that require a management decision.

Return after the next assignment cycle. Did more people hear about the opening in time? Could an employee who was passed over find out what experience would help next time? Ask whether the change made participation easier and what barriers remain. People affected by the arrangement can judge the value of the support. Following their feedback through a second decision often demands more commitment than speaking up at the first one.
Transformative or equity-centered leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
49    Practicing allyship where you have influence
Distinguish a sponsorship decision from a conduct concern

The common case Who gets the visible work? in the leadership styles pathway asks learners to examine both an allocation pattern and what happened when an employee challenged it. Those issues can have different owners and consequences. A person interrupted during a discussion may need immediate support. They may also want the manager to review who gets invited to represent the unit. Correcting the interruption in the next meeting leaves the opportunity structure intact. Changing an invitation list would leave a serious conduct concern unanswered.

Try writing two responses. In the first, step in during the meeting to return the floor and give the employee credit for the point they made. In the second, speak privately afterward. Ask what support the person wants, explain which decisions belong to the supervisor and clarify how any conduct issue will reach the appropriate authorized process. Avoid promises about confidentiality or the outcome that exceed your authority. A colleague acting as an ally can offer to support the employee while allowing them to speak in their own words.

Next, investigate how visible assignments move from a supervisor's desk to a person's workload. Recruitment by informal conversation can favor staff who work nearby, have time to volunteer or already know a temporary opportunity is likely. People who have covered difficult work behind the scenes may have relevant qualifications that remain unseen. Examine how eligibility was defined, who learned about the assignment, who had preparation and what decisions were documented. Respect privacy as you trace the procedure.
Use influence where a decision can change

The Transformative or equity-centered leadership lesson invites attention to how a system distributes opportunity. In this case, a supervisor might publish selection criteria, offer practice for first-time presenters and account for coverage on staff schedules. Consider who will still be excluded. Employees working a late shift might see a notice only after a slot is full. A rotation may distribute turns but leave all the coaching with one person. Ask staff privately how they learned about the opportunity and what would have made participation feasible.

Agree on a review point after enough assignments have been made to examine a pattern. Record which parts the supervisor can change now and which decisions require another authority. Share the changes and the reason for them in a way that avoids identifying whoever first raised the concern. Ask the people the change was meant to support whether it gave them a choice they could use. Acting as an ally involves accepting that their answer may differ from the leader's assessment of the effort.
Development capability. Develop and sponsor others equitably.
Fair access and inclusion     /     ARTICLE 50
Creating a culture of inclusion

A team invites employees to comment on a proposed service change. During the meeting, staff who answer public calls describe a problem with the revised instructions. Later, the decision memo credits the design group and says employees broadly supported the plan. The invitation was open. The record still erased both the concern and the people who raised it. Inclusion becomes visible in what happens to a contribution after someone makes it.
Widen the ways people can contribute

Explain what people can influence, circulate enough information to think about the question, and use language that gives everyone a way in. Address a group as colleagues or participants. Use the names and pronouns people share. Give directions people can follow whether they use speech, chat, a keyboard, or a mobility aid. A team might say, “The service desk is on the first floor beside the elevators,” so someone can choose a route that works for them. Invite comments privately or in writing as well as during the meeting.

Ask whose knowledge the decision requires. Bring the people doing the work into the discussion at a stage when their experience can change its direction. A senior participant can help by crediting a colleague’s observation by name when appropriate and giving the colleague room to explain it. If someone mocks a question or dismisses an accent, the meeting leader can interrupt, identify the disrespectful behavior, and return the discussion to the person’s point. Follow up through the appropriate workplace process when further action is needed.
Show people what became of their contribution

In the service-change example, the meeting leader can ask the employees to check the account of the problem and invite a different view from staff who read the memo later. The decision owner can explain which instruction will change, who will test the revision, and why another suggestion cannot be adopted now. If the memo misattributed the work, correct the record and share the corrected version with its recipients.

Over several decisions, look for a pattern. Do the same voices carry formal credit while other staff supply evidence in private? Do people learn what happened only if they attend an optional event? Adjust how decisions are recorded and communicated. Trust has a concrete basis when employees can raise a hard point, recognize it in the record, and see who took responsibility for acting on it.
Inclusive leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
50    Creating a culture of inclusion
Give disagreements a place in the decision record

An invitation to contribute has little value if a staff member's concern disappears between the conversation and the final recommendation. A leader can interrupt that pattern while a decision is being made. Put the question in plain language, explain what is still open, and invite different accounts of what might happen after release. Give contributors a chance to check the account of what they said. If people disagree, record the specific point of disagreement and what would help resolve it.

Try this with a public message about a change in service hours. A communications specialist wants a short announcement. A front-desk worker knows callers will ask how to reach someone outside the new hours. A community partner points out that people may depend on a contact who is no longer available. These three people have identified different tasks the message needs to support. Combine an accessible announcement with clear details about what happens when the office is closed, then ask each contributor to try it on the situation they described.

Use Inclusive leadership alongside Democratic or participative leadership in the leadership styles collection. Rehearse two versions of the decision meeting. In the first, everyone has equal speaking time but only the manager decides what is recorded. In the second, participants can offer written comments, review the options and correct the record before the manager makes the choice. Ask who could influence the outcome in each version and which conditions made their expertise visible. A vote can be useful for some choices. It is a poor way to decide whether an individual experienced exclusion.
Make trust visible after the decision

Language matters throughout this work. An invitation that addresses “everyone,” names the task and explains ways to participate gives people less to infer about whether they belong. Credit the person or group responsible for an improvement, checking their preferences when a public acknowledgment would identify someone who raised a sensitive concern. If a supervisor uses inaccurate wording or overlooks a contribution, correct the record while the people affected can still use the correction.

Use Find out what changed in practice after the revised message goes out. Ask whether staff could give a usable answer to the after-hours question and whether the partner agrees that the revised directions reflect the concern. Share what the team learned and what it will revisit. Over several decisions, look for who is consistently consulted early enough to influence the options. If one unit only gets invited to comment after decisions appear settled, change when it enters the process as well as how its staff are invited.
Development capability. Connect equity with workforce decisions.
