Using pronouns respectfully

You are about to introduce a colleague who will lead a discussion with community partners. You know the person’s name and role. You have heard colleagues use different pronouns for them. The introduction needs a few ordinary, accurate words. “Jordan Lee will lead today’s discussion. Jordan coordinates the partner meetings” works while you find a suitable opportunity to check how the person would like to be introduced.
Ask in a way that leaves room to choose

Pronouns such as she, he, and they let us refer to a person without repeating a name. Someone’s name, voice, or appearance cannot reliably tell you which pronouns they use. If it is relevant, ask the person privately, or offer your own pronouns when making an introduction. A simple question is enough. “How would you like me to introduce you to this group?” gives Jordan room to mention pronunciation, pronouns, title, or simply the name that should appear on the agenda.

People may choose different ways of introducing themselves in different settings. If someone has told you their pronouns in a private conversation, check how they want you to refer to them with the public or in written materials when the setting is uncertain. Give participants the option of sharing pronouns during introductions. Include anyone who chooses to pass and keep the meeting moving. A colleague should be able to participate fully without explaining a personal decision.
Use what the person shares and repair a mistake

Once Jordan shares that they use they and them with the group, practice with a sentence tied to the work. “Jordan reviewed the questions. They will invite partners to speak first.” If you use the wrong pronoun, offer a brief apology, correct the phrase, and continue. An extended explanation can leave your colleague trying to reassure you in front of an audience. If an incorrect introduction was sent in writing, ask how best to correct it and reach the people who received it.

Supervisors shape what happens after the correction. Use the right pronouns yourself, attend to repeated disrespect, and follow up with the employee about support. Staff can build fluency privately, using ordinary work sentences until the words come naturally. Everyday use spares the person the burden of correcting the same mistake at every meeting.
Ethical leadership
Course and competency crosswalk
51    Using pronouns respectfully
Distinguish the person's words from a workplace assumption

Before a public meeting, an organizer may receive a biography, a directory entry and an introduction from another team. Each may have been written for a different audience or at a different time. Use the wording the speaker supplied for this event when it is available. When materials differ, contact the speaker privately with a practical question about the introduction. They may provide pronouns, ask to use a name throughout, or simply approve a short introduction. Organizers can prepare accurately while giving the speaker authority over how much personal information to share.

Consider a supervisor preparing to introduce Jordan to a community group. The agenda will be posted publicly, but the planning email stayed within a small team. A colleague suggests putting pronouns after every name to show that the event is welcoming. An inclusive response gives each presenter the opportunity to supply the wording used publicly. That allows presenters to share what they choose without making disclosure a condition of appearing on the agenda. It also removes the need for staff to infer anything from a person's voice, clothing or name.

Practice writing complete sentences in the context of the person's work. If someone uses they and them, rehearse both a subject and an object sentence about the work they will lead. Say the sentences aloud until they sound ordinary. Practice with invented examples or in your own notes. A colleague who has supplied their pronouns has already provided the information needed and need not coach the rest of the team.
Decide what an appropriate correction requires

A spoken mistake in an introduction can usually be corrected at once. A mistake in an invitation that was sent to multiple organizations raises another question. Which correction will reach the people who need accurate information while respecting the speaker's wishes? Talk privately with the speaker where possible. A corrected agenda may suffice. A public explanation about a private matter could create a new problem. Ask the person who manages the event materials to check where the outdated version was also posted.

Use Ethical leadership in the leadership styles collection to examine a harder case in which someone repeatedly dismisses a colleague's correction. Describe the observable behavior and its effect on participation. A supervisor can restate the expectation for respectful conduct, offer appropriate support privately and follow the workplace process that fits the concern. Staff should not have to settle the matter in a public debate. In a rehearsal, judge the supervisor's response by whether it protects the colleague's dignity, corrects the working practice and gives the person a reliable route for follow-up. The colleague's willingness to explain their identity is unrelated to the supervisor's responsibility to act.
Development capability. Communicate and facilitate across difference.
Leadership styles in practice

Choose a style to examine how a leader uses authority, who can challenge a decision and what follows for staff and the people they serve. The examples are learning situations. Describe the decision and its consequences before choosing an approach.
Authority and accountability
Authoritarian leadership
Autocratic or directive leadership
Bureaucratic or procedural leadership
Transactional leadership
Ethical leadership
Influence and organizational change
Charismatic leadership
Transformational leadership
Transformative or equity-centered leadership
Adaptive and situational leadership
Participation and development
Democratic or participative leadership
Servant leadership
Laissez-faire leadership
Empowering or delegative leadership
Coaching or developmental leadership
Shared or distributed leadership
Inclusive leadership
Authoritarian leadership

In this pathway, authoritarian leadership means a leader keeps authority by demanding obedience, limiting challenge and attaching consequences to disagreement. It overlaps with autocratic decision-making. The defining feature here is how the leader treats disagreement. A leader can be firm, set clear rules and make final decisions without being authoritarian. The line is crossed when questions are treated as disloyalty and people learn that speaking up costs them something.
Two caseworkers argue about a new case

Two caseworkers argue in front of the team about who should take a complex new case. One says the other always gets the easier ones. The leader is under deadline pressure. The leader ends the argument by ruling: “Enough. I'll assign it. No more discussion.” The argument stops. The question of how cases are assigned is never answered, and both people learn not to raise workload concerns again.

The leader sets a clear boundary on how the disagreement happens, then makes the decision rule visible: “We won't settle this by arguing in front of the team. I'll assign this case today using our caseload criteria. This week I'll share those criteria with everyone, and you can question them.”
Restore a way to challenge authority

Imagine that the caseworkers comply and never argue in front of you again. That result tells you the instruction changed what staff say in your presence. It tells you very little about workload. Compare case complexity, the support each worker received and what happens to concerns raised privately. Give staff a way to challenge the rule even when you made the original assignment. A test of repaired trust is whether they can raise a difficult exception and see it considered without a loss of opportunity.
Try the decision

You notice that no one on your team has raised a concern in three months. In the last meeting where someone did, you cut them off to stay on the agenda. Write down what someone might reasonably fear would happen if they raised a concern with you. Plan how you will check, in a month, whether people are raising concerns again.
Article 26 · Build psychological safety into daily work
Practice case · The acting lead
Autocratic or directive leadership

The leader keeps decision authority. Unlike the authoritarian pattern, the leader may still consult people and allow respectful disagreement. The key question is what the authority is used for. A directive leader can use authority to investigate and correct a problem, or to close off inquiry. Those are very different leaders, even though both make the decision themselves.
A notice deadline and a translation gap

A program team cannot agree whether to delay a notice to providers so it can be translated. The deadline is in two days. Half the team says the deadline matters most. The other half says the families who most need the notice will not be able to read it. A directive leader breaks the deadlock by deciding. The risk is deciding from the leader's own habits, for example releasing in English only because that is how it has always been done.

“I will confirm the notice requirements and language-access arrangements with the responsible staff before release. We need a plan that meets the deadline and lets affected families understand and act on the notice. If those requirements cannot both be met, I will raise the conflict with the authorized decision-maker now. We will review what happened and improve preparation for the next notice.”
Name the decision that belongs to you

List the decisions hidden in the word “release.” Who can verify the required date? Who can confirm a usable version in the languages needed? Who can authorize a different release plan? Clear direction can stop a mistaken mailing while those questions are resolved. Silence about authority can leave the person nearest the deadline to take a risk on everyone else’s behalf. When the immediate decision is made, tell staff how to challenge an incorrect assumption and who will change the preparation schedule for next time.
Try the decision

Your team's shared calendar shows that only staff who work standard daytime hours have been offered training slots this quarter. You have the authority to change the schedule. Write the decision you can make today, in one or two sentences. Set a date to check the effect and name what you will look at.
Article 36 · Making a decision when the cause is uncertain
Practice case · The online intake form
Democratic or participative leadership

People affected by a decision help shape it. Participation does not have to mean everyone agrees or the majority votes. It means people's input can change the result. Good participation is honest about limits: what people can influence, what is fixed, who decides, and how input will be used.
Moving the team meeting

Staff disagree about moving the weekly team meeting from in person to hybrid. Some staff with long commutes or caregiving duties want a hybrid option. Others say the meeting works better in one room. A participative leader brings the team into the decision. The risk is a simple majority vote, where the people facing access barriers are outvoted.

The leader sets the boundary first: “Everyone on this team must be able to take part fully. That part is not up for a vote. Within that, help me design the format.” The leader offers a private way to give input, decides, and then reports back on how the input shaped the result.
Give contributors a decision they can still change

Suppose staff can comment on the meeting format but leadership has already booked every meeting in the same room for the year. What can participation realistically influence? Disclose the booking and ask whether it can be changed. Invite colleagues to identify the tasks that are hard remotely or in person, and let them try workable alternatives. The person facilitating can then explain how specific contributions altered the design. An attendance count alone cannot tell you whether a colleague who shared an access concern had any influence.
Try the decision

Your unit is updating its process for approving training requests. You plan a listening session. Write the five safeguard statements for this decision: what can change, what cannot, who decides, how input is used, and other ways to take part. Decide how and when you will report back what changed.
Article 37 · Working with partners and the public
Practice case · The listening sessions
Servant leadership

The leader puts the growth, well-being and independence of the people they serve first. Robert Greenleaf's description of servant leadership asks whether the people served become freer and more independent, and whether the least privileged benefit or are further deprived. That second question makes servant leadership an equity question, not only a kindness question.
The informal interpreter

A newer staff member who speaks Karen is asked, informally, to interpret on every call with Karen-speaking families. A longer-serving colleague says it is “just helping out.” The newer staff member is falling behind on their own work and says so quietly. A servant leader listens closely and wants to support both people. The risk is smoothing things over to keep harmony, for example by thanking the newer staff member and asking them to keep helping.

The leader treats the extra work as real work. They stop informal interpreting assignments, arrange qualified interpreting through the established process, and check whether any staff interpreting role is authorized and appropriately qualified. They recognize the work already done, review the newer staff member's workload, and ask both colleagues what support they need.
Put the cost of helping back on the work plan

A supportive private conversation might give the newer worker a welcome chance to describe what has happened. It leaves the worker in a difficult position if every colleague can still redirect calls to them. The supervisor can change the routing instruction, arrange qualified support through the appropriate channel and protect time for existing assignments. Check the result with the worker and with the public-facing team. Did people reach the service, and could the employee say no to duties outside the agreed role without losing standing?
Try the decision

A staff member tells you they never seem to hear about stretch projects until someone else has already been chosen. Write a first response that offers support without assuming a skill gap. Name one change to the process and one form of support you could offer if the person wants it.
Article 49 · Practicing allyship where you have influence
Practice case · The acting lead
Charismatic leadership

The leader builds commitment through personal presence, storytelling, confidence and emotional connection. Charisma can bring energy and attention to a neglected issue. The risk is that the work depends on the person rather than on clear criteria and shared ownership.
A question in the chat

A popular division leader announces a new community partnership at an all-staff meeting. A staff member asks in the chat whether community members were consulted. The room goes quiet. The leader answers with a moving story about why the partnership matters. The question is treated as negativity. Others who had the same question decide not to ask.

“That's a fair question, and thank you for asking it here. The honest answer is that we talked with two organizations but not with families directly. We will share what consultation happened and add a way for families to shape the next phase. If you have other questions, here is how to send them, with or without your name.”
Make the commitment transferable

A story can bring people into a discussion about why a partnership matters. When a colleague asks who influenced the decision, a story cannot establish who participated. Identify the choices still open and invite the partners to name a decision they can change. Ask someone other than the senior leader to explain what input was received and where it appears in the plan. If progress stalls whenever one popular leader is away, move that knowledge and decision authority to the people who will maintain the relationship.
Try the decision

You are known as an inspiring speaker. You realize that most of the people you have sponsored for leadership roles remind you of yourself at their stage. List the qualities you have used, formally or informally, to judge who is “ready.” Name one opportunity you will open through a visible process instead of a personal invitation.
Article 07 · How colleagues come to trust your leadership
Practice case · The listening sessions
Transformational leadership

The leader motivates people around a vision, challenges existing practice and supports people's development. Transformational leadership can make major redesign possible. But transformation is not equitable by itself. The direction of the change, and who carries its costs, matter.
A thirty-day goal

A unit adopts a new vision: every family gets a decision within 30 days. Staff who serve families who need interpreters say the timeline will push those families to the back of the line. The leader rallies the team behind the goal and treats the concern as resistance to change.

The leader builds the equity outcome into the vision itself: “Thirty days for every family, including families who need an interpreter.” The unit tracks the timeline separately for families who need language or disability access, funds the interpreting needed to meet it, and asks the staff who raised the concern to help shape the rollout.
Test the ambition against the hardest route

A faster average can conceal a longer wait for someone whose appointment requires language support. Before adopting a target, ask which event starts the clock, which stops it and what happens to an unresolved case. Invite staff and people using the service to describe a timely decision they could actually use. A vision becomes operational when the unit can specify what counts, what supports the work requires and who can repair a failure. The service deadline in this example is a proposed teaching target.
Try the decision
You are drafting a one-sentence vision for your unit's next year. Write the vision. Name the resources, owner and measure that would make the rewritten vision real.
Article 35 · Setting a vision people can use
Practice case · The new case model
Transformative or equity-centered leadership

In this pathway, transformative leadership explicitly examines power, inequitable assumptions, institutional arrangements and the distribution of benefits and burdens. It does not presume the answer. It investigates criteria, history, authority and effects, and then changes the rules and resources that create barriers.
Incomplete documentation

A data review shows that Black and American Indian applicants to a support program are denied more often for “incomplete documentation.” Two managers argue. One says staff just follow the rules. The other says the rule is biased. A transformative leader treats the rule itself as a legitimate subject of review, instead of choosing between “the rule is fine” and “the rule is racist.”

The leader asks: Where did this documentation rule come from? Which documents are hardest to get, and for whom? What help do applicants get, and when? Who can change the rule? The leader involves applicants and community partners and checks with the person or area responsible for Tribal relations about any consultation or coordination obligations. With the required approval, the team tests an allowed change, such as accepting other permitted documents or providing help earlier, and checks the results.
Find the point where the burden is imposed

Two applicants may have equal formal access to a process while one has repeated contact with a person who can help gather the documents. Trace one routine route and one more difficult route using de-identified or invented examples. Identify the source and purpose of each requirement, which evidence is permitted, who approves an exception and when help is offered. If staff find a disparity, use it to identify a question worth investigating. Before recommending a remedy, listen to applicants and involve whoever holds authority for the decision.
Try the decision

Your unit uses the phrase “strong communicator” when choosing who represents the team to partners. Write down what the phrase means in practice. What behaviors count? Name who has authority to adopt the change.
Article 47 · Cultural awareness, competence and humility
Practice case · The online intake form
Laissez-faire leadership

In this pathway, passive laissez-faire leadership means avoiding decisions, feedback or intervention when they are needed. It is not simply allowing people independence. Research has associated this passive pattern with workplace stress, bullying and psychological distress. These are associations, not proof that every low-intervention leader causes harm.
Two colleagues stop speaking

Two staff stop speaking to each other after a disagreement over shared work. Others start working around them. Deadlines slip. The leader hopes it will resolve on its own. Over time, informal alliances decide who gets information and help.

The leader names the effect on the work, meets with each person, sets clear expectations for how they will work together, and checks in on a set date. If either person describes conduct that may need a formal response, the leader routes it to the person or area responsible.
Separate independence from abandonment

An experienced worker may reasonably ask for space to settle a routine difference. Establish what the worker can decide, when help will be available and what signs call for a supervisor. If colleagues must carry messages between the two people to keep a case moving, the cost of the conflict has already spread. Meet separately to learn what happened. Decide what can be addressed as a work problem and what requires a different authorized response. Name a time to check whether the handoff works again.
Try the decision

A staff member mentioned a concern to you two weeks ago in passing. You have not followed up. Write what you will say when you follow up, including what you will do and by when. Set one habit that will keep this from happening again, such as a weekly list of open concerns.
Article 19 · When a concern keeps coming back
Practice case · The new case model
Empowering or delegative leadership

The leader shares authority while providing resources, clarity, support and accountability. Delegation can widen influence and build people's skills. It can also shift burdens without real power. The difference is whether the people given responsibility also get authority, time and protection.
A plan overruled

A team is asked to redesign how it schedules home visits. The leader hands the work to three staff. Two weeks later, their plan is overruled by a manager who was never told the group had any authority. Delegation without clear decision rights turns into wasted effort and lost trust.

Before delegating, the leader writes down what the group can decide, what needs approval and from whom, what time they have, and when they will check in. The leader tells the manager in advance and backs the group when its decisions are questioned.
Make the sponsor’s promise usable

Ask a team member to describe what they could do tomorrow if the receiving office refused the proposed schedule. If the only answer is to ask the sponsor to start over, the delegation needs clearer authority. Agree with the receiving manager on what can be decided before asking staff to invest their time. When a new constraint emerges, explain it promptly and reopen only the affected decision. Give credit to the people who did the design, including those whose recommendations challenged the sponsor’s preferences.
Try the decision

You want to delegate the planning of your unit's next community listening session. Write the decision rights: what the group decides, what needs your approval, what is fixed. Name what you will do if someone senior questions the group's plan.
Article 46 · Communicating clearly when you delegate
Practice case · The listening sessions
Transactional leadership

The leader sets standards, monitors performance, and uses recognition, rewards or corrective responses. Transactional practices can make equity commitments concrete. They are only as fair as the standards they enforce.
Who hears about extra hours

Some staff are always offered extra paid hours. Others never hear about them. A staff member who cares for a parent says the offers always come by text late in the day. The leader sets a rule and tracks compliance. The risk is a rule like “first to reply gets the hours,” which rewards whoever can answer fastest.

The leader checks the applicable scheduling rules and bargaining agreement with Human Resources. Within those requirements, the leader makes openings visible, provides an appropriate response window, and reviews who receives offers and who accepts them. The review asks whether short-notice availability is necessary for the work and how the process affects staff with different schedules or caring responsibilities.
Look for who can satisfy the rule

A rule that pays attention only to response speed favors the people who can check a message immediately. Someone may be helping a resident, off shift or away from the office when an opportunity is announced. Before measuring compliance, examine who can meet the rule and why the rule exists. Agree on an invitation window, a reviewable way to allocate hours and a way to explain exceptions. Count both whether notices went out as promised and whether the pattern of access changed.
Try the decision
Your unit has agreed to make development opportunities more visible. Write one measure of completion and one measure of results. Set an owner, a deadline and a review date.
Article 39 · Workload prioritization
Practice case · One budget, two needs
Bureaucratic or procedural leadership

The leader relies on formal criteria, documentation, roles and established processes. Written criteria can reduce arbitrary decisions. But a process can be followed perfectly and still produce unfair results if nobody examines where it came from, who carries its burdens and what its effects are.
Training videos without captions

A Deaf staff member raises a concern that required training videos have no captions. A manager responds that the vendor contract does not require captions. The leader points to the contract and stops there.

The leader recognizes that accessibility obligations are existing requirements, whatever a contract says. The leader routes the concern to the person or area responsible for accessibility, arranges captions or another accessible version now, and makes sure future contracts include captioning. The leader also follows up with the staff member about any training deadline they could not meet.
Identify the authority behind the procedure

Coaching or developmental leadership

The leader uses feedback, reflection, practice and support to strengthen people's skills. Coaching can widen opportunity. It can also become assimilation training, which helps employees conform to dominant preferences instead of questioning those preferences.
“Too emotional”

A supervisor gives an employee who is Latina feedback that she is “too emotional” in meetings, after she pushed back on a policy affecting families who speak Spanish. The coaching focuses on tone. She is coached to “tone it down,” and the policy concern is lost.

The leader separates the content of her concern from the judgment about her style. The leader checks whether the same intensity from other colleagues gets the same label, takes the policy concern seriously on its merits, and offers coaching on influence only if she wants it.
Check which behavior you propose to change

Write down the specific statement the employee made and the policy question it raised. Could a person with a different communication style have raised the same risk and received a different response? Invite a second reviewer to assess the underlying evidence without your description of the speaker. If there is a work-related behavior to discuss, describe what happened, its effect and the opportunity to try a different approach. Assign someone to examine the policy question on its merits even if a feedback conversation also takes place.

Article 25 · Give feedback that changes the next attempt
Practice case · The new case model
Adaptive and situational leadership

These approaches overlap in practice but are not the same. Situational leadership adjusts direction and support to the task and the person's relevant needs. Adaptive leadership helps a group learn its way through problems whose causes or solutions are uncertain, which may require changes in assumptions and relationships. Both separate what needs immediate action from what needs inquiry.
Two people, one policy change

After a policy change, two staff need very different support. One is new and wants step-by-step direction. The other is experienced but disagrees with the change and says it will hurt families in rural areas. A situational leader gives more direction to the new staff member and more room to the experienced one. The risk is treating the experienced person's disagreement as a support need instead of information.

The leader gives each person the support they need, which is the situational part, and treats the disagreement as a possible signal, which is the adaptive part. The leader asks for evidence about rural families, tests the concern, and reports what was learned.
Match support to the task and inquiry to the uncertainty

A practice session may help a new worker apply a policy. It cannot settle whether the policy creates a barrier for families outside a metro area. Set up two different inquiries. Ask the new worker which part of the task needs demonstration, then observe a second attempt. Ask the experienced worker which step they believe will fail, for whom and under what conditions. Invite someone familiar with that setting to help test it. Explain differential support in terms of the task and needs people can bring forward.
Try the decision
You have given one staff member extra flexibility on deadlines and another none. Write the reason for the difference in one sentence. If it fails any of these, decide what to change.

Shared or distributed leadership

Leadership responsibilities and influence are spread across people with relevant expertise and experience. Shared leadership brings neglected knowledge into decisions. Representation without authority, however, becomes tokenism.
A recommendation ignored

A cross-role workgroup recommends changing how interpreter requests are approved. Months pass. Senior leaders never respond. Members conclude that shared leadership was for show, and the people who volunteered stop volunteering.

The charter sets a response date for every recommendation. Leaders accept, change or decline each one in writing, with reasons. Members have time set aside for the work, and their contributions are recognized in performance conversations.
Follow a recommendation past the workgroup

A committee can share responsibility for drafting, while a single office still has authority to accept or reject the result. That arrangement can work if people know it at the outset. Identify what the group can decide, which choices are recommendations, where dissent is recorded and by when the sponsor must answer. Give participants time within their workloads and make it possible to contribute outside the meeting. Ask whether a distinctive piece of knowledge from the workgroup changed a decision and what happened to recommendations the sponsor declined.

You are forming a group to improve how your unit communicates with families. Draft a three-line charter: what the group decides, what it recommends, and when leaders must respond. Check whether the same people are on every group like this, and why.
Article 46 · Communicating clearly when you delegate
Practice case · The listening sessions
Ethical leadership

Ethical leadership emphasizes principled conduct, fair treatment, consistent standards and accountability. Its danger is assuming that a leader's good intentions or personal integrity prove that the institution is fair. A fair person can run an unfair process without knowing it.
A high performer's comments

A manager learns that a high-performing staff member has been making comments about a coworker's accent. The high performer is close to the manager and is leading an important project. The temptation is to handle it lightly or wait until that work is done.

The manager applies the same standard that would apply to anyone. The manager addresses the conduct, follows the authorized process for reporting and responding to it, protects the coworker from retaliation, and does not ask the coworker to smooth things over.
Test consistency when the decision is inconvenient

Imagine learning about the same comments from an employee without close ties to the manager. Would the threshold for action be the same? A useful private check is to ask an authorized colleague about the process and write down the reason for the chosen response. Protect the person who raised the concern from having to prove that the most visible employee on the project is dispensable. Keep the work moving through a separate coverage decision. Return to the reporting employee about support and follow-through within appropriate privacy limits.
Try the decision

Think of a standard you hold your team to, such as meeting deadlines or professional conduct. Recall the last three times the standard was not met. How did you respond each time? Write one commitment that would make your response more consistent.
Article 51 · Using pronouns respectfully
Practice case · Credit and names
Inclusive leadership

Inclusive leadership emphasizes belonging, contribution and valuing differences without requiring people to assimilate. Research on inclusive leadership, including work by Randel and colleagues, highlights belonging and being valued for one's uniqueness. Central behaviors include support, justice and equity, shared decision-making, encouraging diverse contributions, and helping people contribute fully.
Last-minute documents

In planning meetings, the same three people do most of the talking. A staff member who uses a screen reader says shared documents are posted minutes before meetings, in formats she cannot read in advance. A leader focused only on climate thanks her and encourages everyone to “speak up more.”

The leader sends materials in accessible formats at least two days ahead, rotates who facilitates, offers ways to contribute in writing before and after the meeting, and keeps track of whose ideas are adopted.
Trace a person’s opportunity to influence the result

Being able to join a meeting is the first step. A person also needs the material early enough to understand the choice, a usable way to offer a different view and a route to see what happened to it. A manager can ask a colleague to trace one contribution from preparation to final decision. Look for a point where that contribution was altered, lost or taken up. Change the responsible step and invite the colleague to check it at a later meeting, without asking them to manage everyone else’s access.

Article 18 · Plan for the capabilities your team will need
The all-staff meeting

A division holds a hybrid all-staff meeting. A Deaf staff member requested American Sign Language interpreting two weeks earlier. The interpreters were not booked. Live captions are turned off because “they slow down the platform.” A manager suggests sending meeting notes afterward. In the same week, a different staff member tells their supervisor they are having trouble with long video meetings because of a disability and asks whether they could join some meetings by phone or get materials in writing. The supervisor is unsure what to do and asks the team what they think.
The first decision

There are two failures to address. The first employee needs access to a meeting that is happening now. The second has asked for an individual adjustment and a private response. Identify who can immediately restore participation and who can route the second request without disclosing a colleague’s personal information to the team.
Compare two responses

“Let's ask the team whether we should allow phone-in options for meetings.” The supervisor turns one person's accommodation request into a group decision and exposes a private disclosure. Participation is the wrong tool here.

“Thank you for telling me. I'll connect you with the accommodation process today and keep what you've shared private. In the meantime, I'll send written materials ahead of our meetings for everyone.” The supervisor routes the request correctly, protects privacy and makes an immediate change that helps everyone without singling anyone out.

Article 48 · Accessibility in documents and meetings
The listening sessions

A program is redesigning how families learn about a new support option. Leadership prefers a short online survey and the original launch date. In listening sessions, Somali and Latino families, and several disability advocates, ask for in-person sessions in the evening, with interpreters, and for the notice to be rewritten in plain language before launch. Meeting their requests would delay the launch by six weeks. A senior leader says, “We heard them, but we can't let a few voices hold up the whole program.”
The first decision

The families in this case spoke for their own experience. Find out which decisions the agency left open and what a launch on the original date would mean for access. Ask someone with authority to weigh a delay against possible phased changes. Give participants a chance to check whether the account of their contribution is accurate.
Compare two responses

“I know these families. I've worked with them for years. Trust me, they'll be glad we launched on time.” The leader's personal relationship replaces what families actually said. Their input is overruled by the leader's confidence.

“Here is what we heard, and here is what we can change. We can rewrite the notice in plain language and add two evening sessions with interpreters. The launch date can move three weeks, not six. We will come back to you in a month with what happened.” The leader is honest about limits, shows how input changed the decision and commits to reporting back.

Article 37 · Working with partners and the public
The online intake form

A contracted provider changes its intake process. Families must now complete an English-only online form and upload a photo ID before anyone will talk with them. Within two months, referrals from families in Greater Minnesota and from immigrant families drop sharply. Staff disagree. Some say the contract allows the provider to set its own intake process. Others say families are being turned away before anyone hears their needs.
The first decision

The timing of the referral drop deserves investigation. Trace the new route with an approved practice example from first contact through successful intake. Determine which steps remove a person from the count altogether. Include families who stopped trying and the staff who can authorize a different route. A rebound in referrals would still leave the question of completed access open.
Compare two responses
“The contract lets them set their own intake. Nothing we can do.” Compliance with the contract is treated as the end of the question, even though families are being turned away.

“I'm raising this with the contract manager today. Until it's resolved, our staff will help any family who calls us complete intake by phone.” The leader acts within their authority right away and protects families while the formal question is worked out.
Follow the decision
Follow up on referral numbers by group, where privacy allows, and report what changed. How would you know whether access improved?

Article 36 · Making a decision when the cause is uncertain
One budget, two needs

A division has a small one-time budget. One team wants to translate a widely used notice into several more languages. Another team wants to fund training for staff on serving families with disabilities. Both are worthwhile. There is enough money for one. The two team leads are friendly, but the disagreement has become tense. Each believes the other is not taking the needs of the families they serve seriously.
The first decision

Before comparing benefits, identify any obligations that need to be met through existing funds or another authority. Ask for evidence of the particular difficulty each proposal addresses, who can use it and how long the benefit could last. The budget owner should make the reasons visible and give the unfunded proposal a route for reconsideration.

“Let's go with training. I've seen how powerful it can be.” The decision follows the leader's enthusiasm, not criteria or evidence about who benefits.

“Let's agree on the criteria first, before we argue about the options. Then both teams can make their case against the same criteria.” Agreeing on criteria first turns a contest between people into a comparison of options.
Follow the decision

Article 32 · Managing a public budget through the year
The new case model

Two units are merging, and leadership introduces a new model for assigning cases. Many longtime staff say the model ignores what they know about the families they serve. Some newer staff like it. An African American staff member raises detailed concerns in a meeting about how the model will affect families who rely on a consistent worker. The first decision

What happens to an employee’s standing when a leader calls a specific objection disloyal? “Change is hard. We need everyone on board with the vision.” Disagreement is recast as resistance. The concerns, and the label, go unexamined.

“We'll start the new model as planned for most cases, but we'll test it carefully for families who rely on a consistent worker. In eight weeks we'll review what we learned with staff.” The leader moves ahead while treating the concern as information to test, with a time limit and a review.

Report back on what was learned and what changed. What would show staff that disagreement is safe during this change?

Article 23 · Help your team work through a change
Credit and names

At a leadership briefing, a manager presents an analysis and credits the wrong staff member. The two staff members are both Southeast Asian American, and the manager has confused their names before. The staff member who did the analysis hears about it later from a colleague. They say nothing to the manager, but tell a coworker, “It's not the first time.”
The first decision

Correct the attribution where the audience received it. Then look at how the analysis was submitted, whose name was attached and who could identify the correct author before another briefing. Give the staff member a private route for further concerns. Asking them to accept an apology publicly can force them to protect the manager’s standing.
Compare two responses

“I'm terrible with names. Everyone knows that about me!” The response treats a repeated mistake as a charming quirk and avoids its effect on professional recognition. The example calls for examining the pattern; it does not establish the manager's motive.

“I credited the wrong person for your analysis, and I've confused your names before. That's not acceptable, and I'm sorry. I've corrected the credit with everyone who was at the briefing.” The manager names the mistake specifically, takes responsibility without excuses and corrects it where the harm happened.
Follow the decision
Follow up later to see whether trust has been restored, and accept it if it takes time. What makes it safe for a staff member to tell a leader about a mistake like this?

Leadership Training Design, Delivery, and Implementation: A Meta-Analysis
Christina N. Lacerenza, Denise L. Reyes, Shannon L. Marlow, Dana L. Joseph and Eduardo Salas   ·   2017

The authors synthesized leadership training evaluations from 335 independent employee samples. They examined participant reactions, learning, use of skills beyond training, and results. Across the samples, all four types of outcomes improved on average. In comparisons across programs, attention to learning needs, feedback, practice and sessions spread over time were among the features associated with stronger outcomes.
Program design features often occurred together. The comparisons cannot isolate the causal contribution of each feature or specify a single best delivery model for Minnesota DHS.

An aspiring leader rehearses leading a disputed handoff, receives targeted feedback and later leads an actual handoff under supervision. For directors, use a cross-division decision instead. Review the decision record with someone affected and check later whether the agreed change happened.

Leadership training and just-in-time nudges: A field experiment on the transfer of learning into action
Jørgen Skovhus Haunstrup and Ulrich Thy Jensen   ·   2024

Randomized field experiment with 226 public managers in participating Danish job centers. The researchers compared a control group with training combined with different tools for employee development conversations. Employees reported more behaviors associated with transformational leadership following the intervention that paired training with prompts delivered close to a development conversation. The authors linked the result to conversations in which managers and employees discussed goals.

The outcome was employees’ assessment of managers’ behavior in this setting. Resident outcomes, equitable advancement and the independent effect of a Minnesota program would each require their own evidence.

Before a supervisor’s development conversation, provide one prompt about the work an employee will practice and one about what coverage the supervisor can arrange. After the agreed date, ask the employee whether the assignment occurred and whether the feedback let them improve a second attempt.

Making it safe: the effects of leader inclusiveness and professional status on psychological safety and improvement efforts in health care teams
Ingrid M. Nembhard and Amy C. Edmondson   ·   2006

Observational survey of multiple professions in 23 neonatal intensive care units engaged in quality improvement. In units where leaders were seen to invite and value contributions, professional status was less closely related to how safe employees felt taking interpersonal risks. Greater psychological safety was associated with more engagement in improvement work.
A survey can identify relationships. It cannot establish that the leader’s behavior caused the differences. The clinical hierarchy and improvement projects differ from the settings of many DHS teams.

An executive who sponsors a service redesign can ask the staff who handle exceptions to challenge a draft decision before approval. Review which concerns changed the design and ask the staff whether raising an objection exposed them to any downside. Provide a private route for concerns that carry personal risk.

Can Mentoring Help Female Assistant Professors in Economics? An Evaluation by Randomized Trial
Donna K. Ginther, Janet M. Currie, Francine D. Blau and Rachel T. A. Croson   ·   2020

Among eligible applicants to an oversubscribed economics mentoring workshop, places were allocated by random assignment within research areas. Small groups worked with senior mentors and peers on participants’ own work. Relative to the control group, women who received the intervention were more likely to remain in academia and obtain tenure at institutions ranked in the top 30 or 50 in economics. The authors’ corrected analysis retains these findings.

This was a specific workshop for women in research careers. University tenure and advancement in public service use different processes. The trial evaluated the workshop as a whole and cannot identify which mentoring activity produced its effects.

Offer a small mentoring group for individual contributors interested in greater responsibility. Have each person bring a real, nonconfidential work product; a mentor and peers give specific feedback, then the employee’s supervisor arranges a chance to use it. Track who receives the opportunity and what work they subsequently get to lead.

Advancing Health Equity at the Minnesota Department of Health: 2014–2024
Minnesota Department of Health   ·   2026

In a review of ten years of work, the department and partners collected almost 2,000 completed questionnaires and held more than 20 focused conversations. The community survey invited people who had worked with MDH. A community advisory council helped guide a grant application process and review proposals. Improving Pain Communication Between Limited English-Speaking Hmong Patients, Medical Interpreters, and Health Care Providers in Primary Care: A Pilot Study
Maichou Lor and colleagues   ·   2024

Researchers observed 20 usual-care patient–interpreter–provider encounters followed by 20 encounters using a visual aid alongside spoken interpretation. In total, 36 patients, 27 providers and four interpreters participated. Patients and providers showed better mutual understanding of pain severity in the visual-aid phase. Mutual understanding of location and quality did not improve. Participants completed the tool, though how they used some elements differed from the instructions.
The sequential comparison was small, nonrandomized and designed to examine feasibility. It cannot establish clinical efficacy or a universal preference for visual explanations among Hmong speakers.

In a service-design exercise, offer an optional visual explanation alongside language support. Mark L. Wieland and colleagues, Rochester Healthy Community Partnership   ·   2018

Community and academic partners in Rochester co-developed a program delivered by family health promoters. The team randomized 44 families, totaling 151 participants, to immediate or delayed participation and measured diet and activity. After 12 months, adults receiving the program gained 8.6 points on a 100-point dietary quality index compared with a 4.4-point decline among controls. Adolescent dietary quality and physical activity for either age group showed no statistically significant between-group improvement.
The trial tested the whole intervention. It did not isolate the effect of co-design or establish that other settings or outcomes would improve. Nineteen percent were lost to follow-up by 12 months.
